### Post-apartheid: 1994 – present

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_the_Witwatersrand&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Post-apartheid: 1994 – present")]

On 25 February 2000, university management began implementing a policy called "Wits 2001" under which work deemed "non-core" to the functioning of the university (such as cleaning and landscaping) was outsourced to external contractors; the university's academic departments were also restructured: the university's nine faculties were reduced to five, the university's 99 departments were merged into 40 schools, and courses that were deemed redundant following a mass review were cancelled.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-26)

Wits 2001 attracted widespread criticism from the workers and staff affected, as well as from students and other staff. The arguments behind the restructuring were criticised as badly reasoned, and the policy itself was criticised as being regressive and [neoliberal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neoliberalism "Neoliberalism").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-27) The then-vice-chancellor, Professor [Colin Bundy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_Bundy "Colin Bundy"), said in defence of Wits 2001 that "[t]his fundamental reorganisation of both academic activities and support services will equip the University for the challenges of higher education in the 21st Century".[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-web.archive.org-28) Management issued a statement on 30 May 2000 responding to criticism of Wits 2001 from the [National Education, Health and Allied Workers' Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Education,_Health_and_Allied_Workers'_Union "National Education, Health and Allied Workers' Union") (NEHAWU), the largest trade union among Wits employees, in which it defended Wits 2001 as constituting the "outsourcing [of] contracts for certain non-core functions, rather than any shift in ownership relations or governance" contra NEHAWU's claims that it constituted [privatisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Privatization "Privatization"). Management further defended the changes as "improving the financial sustainability of Wits, taking pressure off management and students, and allowing for better academic and support facilities and services".[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-29)

In 2001, the Johannesburg College of Education was incorporated into the university as Wits Education Campus under the national [Department of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Department_of_Education_(South_Africa) "Department of Education (South Africa)")'s plan to reform tertiary education in South Africa.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-JCE-30) In 2003, a student [mall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shopping_mall "Shopping mall"), called the Matrix, was opened in the Student Union Building on East Campus.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-31) The Wits Origins Centre[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-Origins_Centre_-_Wits_University-32) was opened in 2006 by former president Thabo Mbeki and tells the story of life through its exhibitions. This is alongside the Wits Fossil Vault that houses thousands of plant, animal and hominid fossils, including the [Taung Child](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taung_Child "Taung Child"), [Little Foot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Little_Foot "Little Foot") and [Homo naledi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_naledi "Homo naledi").

Five capital projects were also completed over the next ten years - the Wits Art Museum[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-Wits_Art_Museum_-_Wits_University-33) that is home to over 12 000 works of African art, the Wits Science Stadium - an old athletics stadium converted into state-of-the-art chemistry and physics labs on the West Campus,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-34) the 4th quadrant of the Chamber of Mines Building (now called the ARM Building),[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-35) the FNB Building (now the Margo Steele School of Accountancy),[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-36) and the Wits School of Public Health Building[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-37) in Parktown.

In 2015 to 2016, the [FeesMustFall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/FeesMustFall "FeesMustFall") movement and protests resulted in intermittent disruptions of the academic programme for a few weeks at Wits and other leading South African universities with students protesting for free education.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-EWNshutdown-38) From 2018 onwards, stability returned to Wits and the university continued to be ranked first or second on the continent for academic and research excellence.

In 2022, Wits celebrated its centenary,[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-39) which included saw the university raise R4.2 billion from donors and alumni as part of the Centenary Campaign.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-40) This included raising funds for infrastructure, student support, research and the academic project. This included a R150 million endowment from Wits alumnus [Natie Kirsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nathan_Kirsh "Nathan Kirsh"), for deserving "missing middle" students,[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-41) the opening of the [Chris Seabrooke Music Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chris_Seabrooke_Music_Hall "Chris Seabrooke Music Hall"),[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-42) the launch of the Wits Anglo American Digital Dome,[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-Wits_Anglo_American_Digital_Dome-43) and the reopening of the Wits Sterkfontein Caves,[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-44) amongst other projects.

### Coat of arms

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_the_Witwatersrand&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Coat of arms")]

[![Image 9](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/e/e9/Badge_of_SA_School_of_Mines.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Badge_of_SA_School_of_Mines.png)

The badge of the South African School of Mines

The current coat of arms of the university was designed by Professor G. E. Pearse, and edited by Professor W. D. Howie to correct [heraldic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heraldry "Heraldry") inaccuracies, before being accepted by the [State Herald of South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bureau_of_Heraldry "Bureau of Heraldry") in 1972. The design of the coat of arms incorporates a gold background in the upper section of the shield to represent the Witwatersrand gold fields – on which the mining industry that gave rise to the university is based – along with an open book superimposed upon a cogwheel, representing knowledge and industry. The silver wavy bars on the lower section of the shield represent the [Vaal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaal_River "Vaal River") and [Limpopo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limpopo_River "Limpopo River") rivers which form the northern and southern borders of the Witwatersrand gold fields. Above the shield is the head of a [Kudu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greater_Kudu "Greater Kudu"), an antelope typical of the Witwatersrand and the university's mascot. The university's motto, "_Scientia et Labore_", meaning "Through Knowledge and Work" in [Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin "Latin"), appears just below the shield.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-ReferenceB-45)

The university's coat of arms evolved from the badge of the South African School of Mines. This badge consisted of a diamond with a shield superimposed upon it. A prospector's pick and a sledgehammer overlaid with broken ore and a mill appeared on the shield. The South African School of Mines' motto was the same as the university's current one and surrounded the shield.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-ReferenceB-45)

## Governance and Administration

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_the_Witwatersrand&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Governance and Administration")]

As set out in the _Higher Education Act_ (Act No. 101 of 1997)[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-46) and in the Statute of the University of the Witwatersrand,[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-us-cdn.creamermedia.co.za-47) the university is governed by [Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_Council "University Council"). The chancellor of the university is the ceremonial head of the university who, in the name of the university, confers all degrees. The current chancellor is Dr [Judy Dlamini](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Judy_Dlamini "Judy Dlamini"), who spearheads the female Academic Leadership Fellows Programme.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-48) The positions of principal and vice-chancellor are merged, with the vice-chancellor and principal responsible for the day-to-day running of the university and accountable to Council. The current vice-chancellor and principal is Prof. [Zeblon Vilakazi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeblon_Vilakazi "Zeblon Vilakazi"), a nuclear physicist who will lead Wits until 2030. Council is responsible for the selection of all vice-chancellors, deputy vice-chancellors and deans of faculty.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-us-cdn.creamermedia.co.za-47)[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-49)

## Campuses

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_the_Witwatersrand&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: Campuses")]

Main article: [Campuses of the University of the Witwatersrand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campuses_of_the_University_of_the_Witwatersrand "Campuses of the University of the Witwatersrand")

The university spans 480 hectares and is divided into five academic campuses, with the administration building on the Braamfontein [East Campus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campuses_of_the_University_of_the_Witwatersrand#East_Campus "Campuses of the University of the Witwatersrand"). Across the [De Villiers Graaff Motorway](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M1_(Johannesburg) "M1 (Johannesburg)") lies the [West Campus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campuses_of_the_University_of_the_Witwatersrand#West_Campus "Campuses of the University of the Witwatersrand"). The two are joined by a brick-paved bridge across the highway called the Sibanye-Stillwater Bridge.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-50) East and West Campus effectively form a single campus, bordered by Empire Road to the north, Jan Smuts Avenue to the east, Jorissen Street and Enoch Sontonga Road to the south and Annet Road to the west. The historic East Campus is primarily the home of the faculties of Science and Humanities, as well as Solomon Mahlangu House where the university's Council, Senate and management meet. West Campus houses the faculties of Engineering and the Built Environment, and Commerce, Law and Management. East Campus is home to four residences, namely Men's Res (male), Sunnyside (female), International House (mixed) and Jubilee Hall (female).[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-51) West Campus is home to David Webster Hall (female), Barnato Hall and West Campus Village (both mixed).[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-52)

Wits has three more academic campuses, all located in [Parktown](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campuses_of_the_University_of_the_Witwatersrand#Parktown_Campuses "Campuses of the University of the Witwatersrand"). The Wits Education Campus houses the Wits School of Education,[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-53) within the Faculty of Humanities and boasts three female residences, forming the Highfield cluster, namely Girton, Medhurst and Reith Hall. To the east of the Wits Education Campus (across York Road) lies the Faculty of Health Sciences[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-54) that houses the Wits Medical School and the [Philip V. Tobias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phillip_Tobias "Phillip Tobias") Building, which is the Faculty's administration building. To the West of the Wits Education Campus (across Victoria Avenue) lies the Wits Management Campus, with the triple accredited Wits Business School.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-55) Within the Wits Management Campus are the Ernest Oppenheimer Hall (male residence) and the mixed Parktown Village.

Other residences include Graduate Lodge, Campus Lodge, South Court, Noswal Hall and Braamfontein Centre; all in the city district of Braamfontein and all mixed gender. Further, there is the Wits Junction (mixed) and the Knockando Halls of Residence (a male residence located on the grounds of a [Parktown mansion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parktown_mansions "Parktown mansions") called _Northwards_) in Parktown.

The University of the Witwatersrand houses two [provincial heritage sites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provincial_heritage_sites_(South_Africa) "Provincial heritage sites (South Africa)") and two [heritage objects](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Heritage_objects_(South_Africa) "Heritage objects (South Africa)"). The Great Hall (technically the façade of the Robert Sobukwe Building, formerly known as Central Block, in which the Great Hall is located),[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-56) and the [Dias Cross](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bartholomew_Dias "Bartholomew Dias") housed in the William Cullen Library[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-57) are both [provincial heritage sites](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provincial_heritage_site_(South_Africa) "Provincial heritage site (South Africa)"). [[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_the_Witwatersrand&action=edit&section=12 "Edit section: Cradle of Humankind")]

Main article: [Cradle of Humankind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cradle_of_Humankind "Cradle of Humankind")

[![Image 10](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e1/Homo_naledi_skeletal_specimens.jpg/250px-Homo_naledi_skeletal_specimens.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Homo_naledi_skeletal_specimens.jpg)

[Homo naledi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_naledi "Homo naledi"), discovered by a Wits-based team of palaeontologists working in the Cradle of Humankind

Wits acquired the Sterkfontein and Swartkrans sites in the 1960s, both of which were rich in fossil remains of early [hominids](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hominidae "Hominidae").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-ReferenceA-1) In 1999, the area was declared a [World Heritage Site](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Heritage_Site "World Heritage Site") by [UNESCO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UNESCO "UNESCO") as the _Cradle of Humankind_. As a World Heritage Site, responsibility for the site shifted from the university to the government of [Gauteng Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauteng_Province "Gauteng Province"), with the provincial government becoming the designated management authority responsible for developing and protecting the site. It is aided by the South African Heritage Resources Agency, which has also declared the area a national heritage site.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-62) The university's Evolutionary Studies Institute within the Faculty of Science, continues to play a leading part in excavations of the site and Wits retains ownership of Sterkfontein and its intellectual rights.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-63) Professor [Lee Berger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lee_Rogers_Berger "Lee Rogers Berger") discovered [Australopithecus sediba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australopithecus_sediba "Australopithecus sediba") (2010) and [Homo naledi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_naledi "Homo naledi") (2015) at the site.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-Berger1-64)[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-Berger2015-65) The Wits Sterkfontein Caves reopened to the public in 2025, where Dr Ron Clarke excavated Little Foot. ### Johannesburg Planetarium now the Wits Anglo American Digital Dome

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_the_Witwatersrand&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Johannesburg Planetarium now the Wits Anglo American Digital Dome")]

Main article: [Johannesburg Planetarium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannesburg_Planetarium "Johannesburg Planetarium")

The Johannesburg Planetarium was the first full-sized [planetarium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Planetarium "Planetarium") in Africa and the second in the [southern Hemisphere](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Hemisphere "Southern Hemisphere"). It was originally bought by the Johannesburg municipality to be set up as part of the celebration of the city's seventieth anniversary. After acquiring an old projector from the [Hamburg Planetarium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamburg_Planetarium "Hamburg Planetarium"), which was modernised before being shipped to South Africa, the municipality sold the projector to the university for use as both an academic facility for the instruction of students, and as a public amenity. Plans for a new building to house the projector were first drawn up in 1958, and construction began in 1959. The planetarium finally opened on 12 October 1960.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-69) The Johannesburg Planetarium was often consulted by the media, and the public, in order to explain unusual occurrences in the skies over South Africa.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-70)[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-71) In 2010, the Johannesburg Planetarium celebrated its golden jubilee.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-72)

The Planetarium was closed and was transformed into a Digital Dome which opened its doors to the public in February 2025. The planetarium was renamed to the Wits Anglo American Digital Dome.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-Wits_Anglo_American_Digital_Dome-43)

### Wits Theatre

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_the_Witwatersrand&action=edit&section=16 "Edit section: Wits Theatre")]

Main article: [Wits Theatre Complex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wits_Theatre_Complex "Wits Theatre Complex")

The Wits Theatre is a [performing arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Performing_arts "Performing arts") complex within the university.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-Wits_Theatre-74) It is run by the Wits School of Arts. Prior to the opening of the Wits Theatre, the Wits Schools of Dramatic Art and Music had been staging productions in a building on campus called the Nunnery, a former convent. The Nunnery has been retained as a teaching venue.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-Wits_Theatre-74) A new building, the Wits Seabrooke Music Hall[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-75) was built alongside, and was opened in 2022.

### Wits Centre for Diversity Studies (WiCDS)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_the_Witwatersrand&action=edit&section=17 "Edit section: Wits Centre for Diversity Studies (WiCDS)")]

Main article: [Wits Centre for Diversity Studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wits_Centre_for_Diversity_Studies "Wits Centre for Diversity Studies")

The Wits Centre for Diversity Studies (WiCDS) was established in 2014 at the University of Witwatersrand. It is based in the Faculty of Humanities and aims to build capacity to meet the challenges of diverse societies, especially in [post-apartheid South Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_South_Africa_(1994%E2%80%93present) "History of South Africa (1994–present)") through interdisciplinary postgraduate education and research.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-76)

## Academics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_the_Witwatersrand&action=edit&section=18 "Edit section: Academics")]

### Faculties

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_the_Witwatersrand&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: Faculties")]

The university consists of five faculties: Commerce, Law and Management; [Engineering and the Built Environment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faculty_of_Engineering_and_the_Built_Environment_(University_of_the_Witwatersrand) "Faculty of Engineering and the Built Environment (University of the Witwatersrand)"); [Health Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faculty_of_Health_Sciences_(University_of_the_Witwatersrand) "Faculty of Health Sciences (University of the Witwatersrand)"); [Humanities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faculty_of_Humanities_(University_of_the_Witwatersrand) "Faculty of Humanities (University of the Witwatersrand)"); and [Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faculty_of_Science_(University_of_the_Witwatersrand) "Faculty of Science (University of the Witwatersrand)")[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-77) comprising 33 schools.

### Libraries

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_the_Witwatersrand&action=edit&section=20 "Edit section: Libraries")]

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5c/Wartenweiler_behind_packed_Library_Lawns.jpg/250px-Wartenweiler_behind_packed_Library_Lawns.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wartenweiler_behind_packed_Library_Lawns.jpg)

The Wartenweiler Library, on the south-eastern side of the Library Lawns on East Campus

The University of the Witwatersrand Library Service consists of two main libraries, the Warteinweiler and William Cullen libraries on East Campus, and 12 branch libraries. The **Wartenweiler Library** primarily serves the Faculty of Humanities. It also contains the Library Administration, Library Computer Services and Technical Services departments as well as the Short Loan collection, the Reference collection, Inter-library Loans department, the Multimedia Library, and the Education and Training department as well as the Electronic Classroom.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-78) The **William Cullen Library** contains the Africana collection, specialising in social, political and economic history. It also contains the Early and Fine Printed Books collection, which includes the Incunabula (books printed before 1501). Finally, it also contains a collection of Government Publications and journals in the [arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arts "Arts"), [humanities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Humanities "Humanities") and [social sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_science "Social science").[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_the_Witwatersrand#cite_note-79)

| El Anatsui |

| Known for | [Visual Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_Art "Visual Art"), [Sculpture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sculpture "Sculpture") |

**El Anatsui** ([/ɛ l ˌ æ n ə t ˈ s uː i/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); born 4 February 1944)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-3) is a Ghanaian [sculptor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sculptor "Sculptor") active for much of his career in Nigeria. He has drawn particular international attention for his "[bottle-top](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bottle_cap "Bottle cap") installations". These installations consist of thousands of [aluminum pieces sourced](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium_recycling "Aluminium recycling") from alcohol recycling stations and sewn together with copper wire, which are then transformed into metallic cloth-like wall sculptures. Such materials, while seemingly stiff and sturdy, are actually free and flexible, which often helps with manipulation when installing his sculptures.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-5)

Anatsui was included in the 2023 [_Time_ 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_100 "Time 100") list of the world's most influential people.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:6-6) In the article, artist and art historian Okeke-Agulu writes, "The breathtaking combination of experimental rigor and inspired vision turns such unassuming materials as printer's plates or liquor-bottle caps into the magnificent constructions and compositions displayed around the world."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:6-6)

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

El Anatsui was born in [Anyako](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anyako "Anyako"), in the [Volta Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volta_Region "Volta Region") of Ghana. The youngest of his father's 32 children, Anatsui lost his mother and was raised by his uncle. His first experience with art was through drawing letters on a chalkboard.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:3-7) His lettering attempts drew the attention of his school's headmaster, who encouraged his effort by providing him with more chalk. Because of his age at the time (just after kindergarten), he regarded the letters more as images than as letters--the forms interested him.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:4-8)

Anatsui received his B.A in 1968 from the [College of Art and Built Environment (KNUST)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_of_Art_and_Built_Environment_(KNUST) "College of Art and Built Environment (KNUST)") in Kumasi, Ghana. He received his postgraduate diploma in Art Education the following year, in 1969, from [Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kwame_Nkrumah_University_of_Science_and_Technology "Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology"), also in Kumasi.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:5-9)

Some of his early artistic influences include [Oku Ampofo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oku_Ampofo "Oku Ampofo"), [Vincent Akwete Kofi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_Kofi "Vincent Kofi"), and [Kofi Antubam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kofi_Antubam "Kofi Antubam"), all of whom began to reject foreign influences in their practices in favor of indigenous art forms.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-10) After graduating in 1969, Anatsui assumed a teaching position at Winneba Specialist Training College (now [University of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Education,_Winneba "University of Education, Winneba")), a role that had previously been filled by Kofi.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:3-7)

He began teaching at the [University of Nigeria, Nsukka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria "University of Nigeria") in 1975.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-NMOAA-11) He became a senior lecturer for the Fine and Applied Arts department in 1982, and later became head of that department and full professor of sculpture in 1996, a role he occupied until 2011.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:5-9) His presence at the University of Nsukka led to his affiliation with the [Nsukka group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nsukka_group "Nsukka group").

> It has taken many years to find artists who can occupy a prominent place on the global circuit while choosing to reside outside the [metropolitan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_area "Metropolitan area") centres. [William Kentridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Kentridge "William Kentridge") has made his reputation from [Johannesburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannesburg "Johannesburg"), and El Anatsui has conquered the planet while living and working in the Nigerian university town of Nsukka.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-12)

## Artwork

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Artwork")]

Anatsui notes that, through school and in university, "everything we were doing was western," especially within the fine arts department of his university; he felt that there was something missing in his education for its lack of focus on his own culture.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:2-13) In order to rectify this, he started visiting the National Cultural Centre of Ghana, also in Kumasi, to engage with the musicians, graphic artists, textile artists, printers, and creative artists of all types. It was there that he encountered [Adinkra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adinkra_symbols "Adinkra symbols"), a system of signs and symbols, which was his first introduction to abstract art and opened up a new world of artistic possibilities for him.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:2-13)

In the 1970s, Anatsui worked frequently in wood. He was particularly interested in wooden trays, which he often saw used in the markets to display food items and other wares--he would carve them or engrave them with Adinkra symbols and other marks using hot rods.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:4-8) He also began using wood to construct wall panels from strips placed next to each other, the surface decorated with designs imparted on the material through the use of chain saws, gouges, flame, or paint.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-NMOAA-11) In the late 70s, he began working in clay: pots, in particular, exploring themes of fragility and dilapidation. He was interested in how, even after a pot breaks and ceases being used in the way we commonly think (for food, water), it takes on a new purpose, even acquires more uses, from the mundane to the spiritual. Most intriguing to him is the use of pot shards for presenting offerings. He said, "It's as if the pot, having broken, is transformed into a dimension which makes it ideal for use by ancestors and deities who are themselves in the spirit dimension."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:4-8)

After his work with the broken pots, Anatsui explored food-adjacent themes in other materials: wood, again, in the form of mortars; equipment used to process [cassava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassava "Cassava"), and bottle tops.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:4-8)

Much of Anatsui's work features found materials, or materials that had a life of use prior to being formed into this artworks. His emphasis on the found object, however, is less [Duchampian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcel_Duchamp "Marcel Duchamp"), and more focused on the history of use and the evidence of the human hand in the material.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:4-8)

> "When something has been used, there is a certain charge, a certain energy, that has to do with the people who have touched it and used it and sometimes abused it. This helps to direct what one is doing, and also to root what one is doing in the environment and the culture."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:2-13)

Metal bottle caps are a favorite material of his; like cloth, Anatsui describes, an arrangement of bottle caps is versatile, allowing him to consider his art both sculpturally (through the form of the caps) and in a painterly manner (through the colors of the caps). Further, he appreciates the glimpse that bottle caps give into current and historical political and sociological issues, by virtue of the names and colors of various drink brands that are printed onto the caps.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:2-13)

> "The most important thing for me is the transformation. The fact that these media, each identifying a brand of drink, are no longer going back to serve the same role but are elements that could generate some reflection, some thinking, or just some wonder. This is possible because they are removed from their accustomed, functional context into a new one, and they bring along their histories and identities."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:4-8)

A number of themes are present in Anatsui's work: the destruction and subsequent reconstitution of material as a metaphor for life and the changes Africa faced under colonialism and since independence; traditional themes and motifs of West African strip woven cloth and other [African textiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_textiles "African textiles"); and concern over Western scholarly misinterpretation of African history and the distortions it has caused.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-NMOAA-11) His work is also thematically connected to the West African cultural landscape and ideas of consumption and labor.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:4-8)

The idea of [Sankofa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sankofa "Sankofa") [translated as "go back and retrieve"] is also present in Anatsui's work. He views it as a way of drawing on the past, the lessons it offers, to chart a mode of moving forward. For him, Sankofa described a need to draw from what was immediately around him; Ghana became independent when he was in high school, and much of his education had been focused on western art and art history, and so he felt called to 'go back and retrieve' aspects of Ghanaian culture that had been suppressed, something he described as a sort of "quest for self-discovery."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:4-8)

## Exhibitions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Exhibitions")]

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8f/El_Anatsui_-_Man%27s_Cloth.jpg/250px-El_Anatsui_-_Man%27s_Cloth.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:El_Anatsui_-_Man's_Cloth.jpg)

_Man's Cloth_ (1998–2001) at the [British Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Museum "British Museum") in 2009

Anatsui's career grew gradually, starting in his home village of [Nsukka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nsukka "Nsukka") before branching off to places such as [Enugu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enugu_(city) "Enugu (city)") and [Lagos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagos "Lagos"), and eventually internationally.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14) In 1990, Anatsui had his first important group show at the [Studio Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studio_Museum_in_Harlem "Studio Museum in Harlem") In [Harlem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harlem "Harlem"), [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)"). He also was one of three artists singled out in the 1990 exhibition "Contemporary African Artists: Changing Traditions", which was extended for five years.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14) Anatsui has since exhibited his work around the world, including at the [Brooklyn Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Museum "Brooklyn Museum") (2013);[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-15) the [Clark Art Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clark_Art_Institute "Clark Art Institute") (2011);[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-16) the Rice University Art Gallery, Houston (2010);[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-17) the [Metropolitan Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Museum_of_Art "Metropolitan Museum of Art"), New York (2008–09);[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-18) the [National Museum of African Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_African_Art "National Museum of African Art"), Smithsonian Institution, Washington, D.C. (2008);[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-19) the [Fowler Museum at UCLA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fowler_Museum_at_UCLA "Fowler Museum at UCLA") (2007);[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-20) the [Venice Biennale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice_Biennale "Venice Biennale") (1990 and 2007);[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-interview-21) the [Hayward Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hayward_Gallery "Hayward Gallery") (2005);[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-22) the [Liverpool Biennial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool_Biennial "Liverpool Biennial") (2002);[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-interview-21) the National Museum of African Art (2001);[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-interview-21) the [Centre de Cultura Contemporània de Barcelona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centre_de_Cultura_Contempor%C3%A0nia_de_Barcelona "Centre de Cultura Contemporània de Barcelona") (2001);[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-interview-21) the 8th Osaka Sculpture Triennale (1995);[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-interview-21) the 5th [Gwangju Biennale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gwangju_Biennale "Gwangju Biennale") (2004); the [Arab Museum of Modern Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_Museum_of_Modern_Art "Arab Museum of Modern Art") in Doha (2019);[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-Lucas_40-23) and the [Kunstmuseum Bern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kunstmuseum_Bern "Kunstmuseum Bern") (2020).[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-24) In 1995, Anatsui held his first solo exhibition outside of Africa in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"). He expressed a variety of themes and demonstrated how African art can be shown in a multitude of ways that are not seen as "typical" African.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14) His work utilized conceptual modes used by European and American artists but hardly in African countries.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14) Anatsui showed his work at the de Young Museum in [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco") in 2005. This was his first time "appear[ing] as part of the permanent collection in a major art museum".[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:0-25) Also in 2005, his exhibition at New York's [Skoto Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skoto_Gallery?action=edit&redlink=1 "Skoto Gallery (page does not exist)"), _Danudo_, was the first display of his metal sheets in an American city.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:0-25) At this gallery, Skoto Aghahowa presented Anatsui's wood wall panels alongside [Sol LeWitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sol_LeWitt "Sol LeWitt")'s drawings. This exhibition popularized his bottle-cap works as he gained more recognition in the press.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:0-25)

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/68/Artempo_ElAnatsui.jpg/250px-Artempo_ElAnatsui.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Artempo_ElAnatsui.jpg)

Anatsui's [Palazzo Fortuny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Fortuny "Palazzo Fortuny") Artempo exhibition in 2007

Anatsui was invited to the [Venice Biennale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice_Biennale "Venice Biennale") in 2006 and again in 2007 where he was commissioned to make two hanging metal tapestries. During the 2007 edition, he exhibited his works at the [Palazzo Fortuny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Fortuny "Palazzo Fortuny") which consisted of newly built walls for him to display three metal hangings entitled _Dusasa_.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:0-25) Each artwork demonstrated different textures and colors including golds, reds, and blacks. The way the bottle tops draped throughout the hangings created a sense of gentleness that made it stand apart from the other works in the gallery.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:0-25) The art curator of the Biennale, [Robert Storr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Storr_(art_academic) "Robert Storr (art academic)"), mentions that the artist's series "reaches back into a whole series of things in the postwar period-it has a kind of exaltation I have not seen before".[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:0-25) During this Venetian showing, Anatsui wanted to create a new experience for his viewers conceptually. He believes that "human life is not something which is cut and dried. It is something that is constantly in a state of change."[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14) At this point, he began to refer his metalworks as hangings instead of "cloths".[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14)

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/f/f5/Another_Man%27s_Cloth%2C_2006%2C_El_Anatsui_at_Rubell_DC_2022.jpg/250px-Another_Man%27s_Cloth%2C_2006%2C_El_Anatsui_at_Rubell_DC_2022.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Another_Man's_Cloth,_2006,_El_Anatsui_at_Rubell_DC_2022.jpg)

_Another Man's Cloth_ (2006) at the [Rubell Museum DC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubell_Museum#Rubell_Museum_DC "Rubell Museum") in 2022

A 2010 retrospective of his work, entitled _When I Last Wrote to You About Africa_, was organized by the [Museum for African Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_for_African_Art "Museum for African Art") and opened at the [Royal Ontario Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Ontario_Museum "Royal Ontario Museum") in [Toronto, Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto "Toronto"), Canada. It subsequently toured venues in the United States for three years, concluding at the [University of Michigan Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Michigan_Museum_of_Art "University of Michigan Museum of Art").

A major exhibition of recent works, entitled _Gravity & Grace: Monumental Works by El Anatsui_, had its [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") premiere at the [Brooklyn Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Museum "Brooklyn Museum") in 2013. Organized by the [Akron Art Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akron_Art_Museum "Akron Art Museum") (exhibition: 2012), the exhibition later traveled to the [Des Moines Art Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Des_Moines_Art_Center "Des Moines Art Center") (2013–14) and the [Bass Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bass_Museum "Bass Museum") in Miami (2014).[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-26)

A career-spanning survey of his work, organized by [Okwui Enwezor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okwui_Enwezor "Okwui Enwezor") and [Chika Okeke-Agulu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chika_Okeke-Agulu "Chika Okeke-Agulu"), entitled _Triumphant Scale_ drew record-breaking crowds when it opened in March 2019, at Munich's [Haus der Kunst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haus_der_Kunst "Haus der Kunst"). From there, the show travelled to the [Arab Museum of Modern Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_Museum_of_Modern_Art "Arab Museum of Modern Art"), in Doha, and later to the [Kunstmuseum Bern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kunstmuseum_Bern "Kunstmuseum Bern") in 2020.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-Lucas_40-23)

Anatsui was selected for the 2023 Hyundai Commission at the Turbine Hall at [Tate Modern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tate_Modern "Tate Modern"); a vast display space for large-scale sculptural and site-specific artworks. His work, _Behind the Red Moon_, is made of thousands of metal bottle tops and fragments, building upon his work with materials linked to the transatlantic slave trade, and was on view through 14 April 2024.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-29)

## Other activities

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Other activities")]

Anatsui was selected to be a member of the International Society for Education through Art (InSEA) world council in 1992 for his work in education.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14) Anatsui was a founding member and fellow of the [Forum for African Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forum_for_African_Arts?action=edit&redlink=1 "Forum for African Arts (page does not exist)") in 2000. That year he also became a member of the International Selection Committee for the [Dakar Biennale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dakar_Biennale "Dakar Biennale") in Senegal.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14) In 2001 he was a fellow at the [Civitella Ranieri Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civitella_Ranieri_Foundation "Civitella Ranieri Foundation") in Italy.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:1-30)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14)

## Recognition

### Awards

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Awards")]

Anatsui won an honorable mention at the First [Ghana National Art Competition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghana_National_Art_Competition?action=edit&redlink=1 "Ghana National Art Competition (page does not exist)") as an undergraduate student in 1968. The following year he was awarded the Best Student of the Year at the [College of Art in Kumasi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_of_Art_in_Kumasi?action=edit&redlink=1 "College of Art in Kumasi (page does not exist)"), Ghana.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14) In 1983 he won a commission for two large public sculptures made of terrazzo-surfaced cement on the [Nsukka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nsukka "Nsukka") campus.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14) He was selected to be one of ten artists invited to the [Zweites Symposium Nordesekkuste](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zweites_Symposium_Nordesekkuste?action=edit&redlink=1 "Zweites Symposium Nordesekkuste (page does not exist)") residency in [Cuxhaven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuxhaven "Cuxhaven"), [West Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Germany "West Germany"), in 1984.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14)

In 1990, Anatsui was invited to the 44th annual [Venice Biennale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice_Biennale "Venice Biennale") show _5 Contemporary African Artists_, where he received an honorable mention.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14) That year he was included in the American documentary _Nigerian Art-Kindred Spirits_.

In 2015, the Venice Biennale awarded Anatsui the [Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice_Biennale#Awards "Venice Biennale").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-32) In 2017, Anatsui was awarded the [Praemium Imperiale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Praemium_Imperiale "Praemium Imperiale"), the first Ghanaian to win this international art prize.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-34)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Ghanaian artist (born 1944)

| El Anatsui |
| --- |
| Born | (1944-02-04) 4 February 1944 (age 82) [Anyako, Volta Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anyako,_Volta_Region "Anyako, Volta Region"), Ghana |
| Known for | [Visual Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_Art "Visual Art"), [Sculpture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sculpture "Sculpture") |
| Awards | [Prince Claus Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Claus_Fund "Prince Claus Fund") |

**El Anatsui** ([/ɛ l ˌ æ n ə t ˈ s uː i/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); born 4 February 1944)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-3) is a Ghanaian [sculptor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sculptor "Sculptor") active for much of his career in Nigeria. He has drawn particular international attention for his "[bottle-top](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bottle_cap "Bottle cap") installations". These installations consist of thousands of [aluminum pieces sourced](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium_recycling "Aluminium recycling") from alcohol recycling stations and sewn together with copper wire, which are then transformed into metallic cloth-like wall sculptures. Such materials, while seemingly stiff and sturdy, are actually free and flexible, which often helps with manipulation when installing his sculptures.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-5)

Anatsui was included in the 2023 [_Time_ 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_100 "Time 100") list of the world's most influential people.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:6-6) In the article, artist and art historian Okeke-Agulu writes, "The breathtaking combination of experimental rigor and inspired vision turns such unassuming materials as printer's plates or liquor-bottle caps into the magnificent constructions and compositions displayed around the world."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:6-6)

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

El Anatsui was born in [Anyako](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anyako "Anyako"), in the [Volta Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volta_Region "Volta Region") of Ghana. The youngest of his father's 32 children, Anatsui lost his mother and was raised by his uncle. His first experience with art was through drawing letters on a chalkboard.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:3-7) His lettering attempts drew the attention of his school's headmaster, who encouraged his effort by providing him with more chalk. Because of his age at the time (just after kindergarten), he regarded the letters more as images than as letters--the forms interested him.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:4-8)

Anatsui received his B.A in 1968 from the [College of Art and Built Environment (KNUST)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_of_Art_and_Built_Environment_(KNUST) "College of Art and Built Environment (KNUST)") in Kumasi, Ghana. He received his postgraduate diploma in Art Education the following year, in 1969, from [Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kwame_Nkrumah_University_of_Science_and_Technology "Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology"), also in Kumasi.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:5-9)

Some of his early artistic influences include [Oku Ampofo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oku_Ampofo "Oku Ampofo"), [Vincent Akwete Kofi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_Kofi "Vincent Kofi"), and [Kofi Antubam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kofi_Antubam "Kofi Antubam"), all of whom began to reject foreign influences in their practices in favor of indigenous art forms.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-10) After graduating in 1969, Anatsui assumed a teaching position at Winneba Specialist Training College (now [University of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Education,_Winneba "University of Education, Winneba")), a role that had previously been filled by Kofi.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:3-7)

He began teaching at the [University of Nigeria, Nsukka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria "University of Nigeria") in 1975.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-NMOAA-11) He became a senior lecturer for the Fine and Applied Arts department in 1982, and later became head of that department and full professor of sculpture in 1996, a role he occupied until 2011.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:5-9) His presence at the University of Nsukka led to his affiliation with the [Nsukka group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nsukka_group "Nsukka group").

> It has taken many years to find artists who can occupy a prominent place on the global circuit while choosing to reside outside the [metropolitan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_area "Metropolitan area") centres. [William Kentridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Kentridge "William Kentridge") has made his reputation from [Johannesburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannesburg "Johannesburg"), and El Anatsui has conquered the planet while living and working in the Nigerian university town of Nsukka.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-12)

## Artwork

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Artwork")]

Anatsui notes that, through school and in university, "everything we were doing was western," especially within the fine arts department of his university; he felt that there was something missing in his education for its lack of focus on his own culture.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:2-13) In order to rectify this, he started visiting the National Cultural Centre of Ghana, also in Kumasi, to engage with the musicians, graphic artists, textile artists, printers, and creative artists of all types. It was there that he encountered [Adinkra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adinkra_symbols "Adinkra symbols"), a system of signs and symbols, which was his first introduction to abstract art and opened up a new world of artistic possibilities for him.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:2-13)

In the 1970s, Anatsui worked frequently in wood. He was particularly interested in wooden trays, which he often saw used in the markets to display food items and other wares--he would carve them or engrave them with Adinkra symbols and other marks using hot rods.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:4-8) He also began using wood to construct wall panels from strips placed next to each other, the surface decorated with designs imparted on the material through the use of chain saws, gouges, flame, or paint.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-NMOAA-11) In the late 70s, he began working in clay: pots, in particular, exploring themes of fragility and dilapidation. He was interested in how, even after a pot breaks and ceases being used in the way we commonly think (for food, water), it takes on a new purpose, even acquires more uses, from the mundane to the spiritual. Most intriguing to him is the use of pot shards for presenting offerings. He said, "It's as if the pot, having broken, is transformed into a dimension which makes it ideal for use by ancestors and deities who are themselves in the spirit dimension."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:4-8)

After his work with the broken pots, Anatsui explored food-adjacent themes in other materials: wood, again, in the form of mortars; equipment used to process [cassava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassava "Cassava"), and bottle tops.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:4-8)

Much of Anatsui's work features found materials, or materials that had a life of use prior to being formed into this artworks. His emphasis on the found object, however, is less [Duchampian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcel_Duchamp "Marcel Duchamp"), and more focused on the history of use and the evidence of the human hand in the material.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:4-8)

> "When something has been used, there is a certain charge, a certain energy, that has to do with the people who have touched it and used it and sometimes abused it. This helps to direct what one is doing, and also to root what one is doing in the environment and the culture."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:2-13)

Metal bottle caps are a favorite material of his; like cloth, Anatsui describes, an arrangement of bottle caps is versatile, allowing him to consider his art both sculpturally (through the form of the caps) and in a painterly manner (through the colors of the caps). Further, he appreciates the glimpse that bottle caps give into current and historical political and sociological issues, by virtue of the names and colors of various drink brands that are printed onto the caps.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:2-13)

> "The most important thing for me is the transformation. The fact that these media, each identifying a brand of drink, are no longer going back to serve the same role but are elements that could generate some reflection, some thinking, or just some wonder. This is possible because they are removed from their accustomed, functional context into a new one, and they bring along their histories and identities."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:4-8)

A number of themes are present in Anatsui's work: the destruction and subsequent reconstitution of material as a metaphor for life and the changes Africa faced under colonialism and since independence; traditional themes and motifs of West African strip woven cloth and other [African textiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_textiles "African textiles"); and concern over Western scholarly misinterpretation of African history and the distortions it has caused.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-NMOAA-11) His work is also thematically connected to the West African cultural landscape and ideas of consumption and labor.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:4-8)

The idea of [Sankofa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sankofa "Sankofa") [translated as "go back and retrieve"] is also present in Anatsui's work. He views it as a way of drawing on the past, the lessons it offers, to chart a mode of moving forward. For him, Sankofa described a need to draw from what was immediately around him; Ghana became independent when he was in high school, and much of his education had been focused on western art and art history, and so he felt called to 'go back and retrieve' aspects of Ghanaian culture that had been suppressed, something he described as a sort of "quest for self-discovery."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:4-8)

## Exhibitions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Exhibitions")]

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8f/El_Anatsui_-_Man%27s_Cloth.jpg/250px-El_Anatsui_-_Man%27s_Cloth.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:El_Anatsui_-_Man's_Cloth.jpg)

_Man's Cloth_ (1998–2001) at the [British Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Museum "British Museum") in 2009

Anatsui's career grew gradually, starting in his home village of [Nsukka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nsukka "Nsukka") before branching off to places such as [Enugu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enugu_(city) "Enugu (city)") and [Lagos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagos "Lagos"), and eventually internationally.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14) In 1990, Anatsui had his first important group show at the [Studio Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studio_Museum_in_Harlem "Studio Museum in Harlem") In [Harlem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harlem "Harlem"), [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)"). He also was one of three artists singled out in the 1990 exhibition "Contemporary African Artists: Changing Traditions", which was extended for five years.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14) Anatsui has since exhibited his work around the world, including at the [Brooklyn Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Museum "Brooklyn Museum") (2013);[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-15) the [Clark Art Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clark_Art_Institute "Clark Art Institute") (2011);[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-16) the Rice University Art Gallery, Houston (2010);[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-17) the [Metropolitan Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Museum_of_Art "Metropolitan Museum of Art"), New York (2008–09);[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-18) the [National Museum of African Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_African_Art "National Museum of African Art"), Smithsonian Institution, Washington, D.C. (2008);[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-19) the [Fowler Museum at UCLA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fowler_Museum_at_UCLA "Fowler Museum at UCLA") (2007);[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-20) the [Venice Biennale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice_Biennale "Venice Biennale") (1990 and 2007);[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-interview-21) the [Hayward Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hayward_Gallery "Hayward Gallery") (2005);[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-22) the [Liverpool Biennial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool_Biennial "Liverpool Biennial") (2002);[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-interview-21) the National Museum of African Art (2001);[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-interview-21) the [Centre de Cultura Contemporània de Barcelona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centre_de_Cultura_Contempor%C3%A0nia_de_Barcelona "Centre de Cultura Contemporània de Barcelona") (2001);[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-interview-21) the 8th Osaka Sculpture Triennale (1995);[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-interview-21) the 5th [Gwangju Biennale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gwangju_Biennale "Gwangju Biennale") (2004); the [Arab Museum of Modern Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_Museum_of_Modern_Art "Arab Museum of Modern Art") in Doha (2019);[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-Lucas_40-23) and the [Kunstmuseum Bern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kunstmuseum_Bern "Kunstmuseum Bern") (2020).[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-24) In 1995, Anatsui held his first solo exhibition outside of Africa in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"). He expressed a variety of themes and demonstrated how African art can be shown in a multitude of ways that are not seen as "typical" African.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14) His work utilized conceptual modes used by European and American artists but hardly in African countries.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14) Anatsui showed his work at the de Young Museum in [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco") in 2005. This was his first time "appear[ing] as part of the permanent collection in a major art museum".[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:0-25) Also in 2005, his exhibition at New York's [Skoto Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skoto_Gallery?action=edit&redlink=1 "Skoto Gallery (page does not exist)"), _Danudo_, was the first display of his metal sheets in an American city.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:0-25) At this gallery, Skoto Aghahowa presented Anatsui's wood wall panels alongside [Sol LeWitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sol_LeWitt "Sol LeWitt")'s drawings. This exhibition popularized his bottle-cap works as he gained more recognition in the press.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:0-25)

[![Image 5](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/68/Artempo_ElAnatsui.jpg/250px-Artempo_ElAnatsui.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Artempo_ElAnatsui.jpg)

Anatsui's [Palazzo Fortuny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Fortuny "Palazzo Fortuny") Artempo exhibition in 2007

Anatsui was invited to the [Venice Biennale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice_Biennale "Venice Biennale") in 2006 and again in 2007 where he was commissioned to make two hanging metal tapestries. During the 2007 edition, he exhibited his works at the [Palazzo Fortuny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Fortuny "Palazzo Fortuny") which consisted of newly built walls for him to display three metal hangings entitled _Dusasa_.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:0-25) Each artwork demonstrated different textures and colors including golds, reds, and blacks. The way the bottle tops draped throughout the hangings created a sense of gentleness that made it stand apart from the other works in the gallery.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:0-25) The art curator of the Biennale, [Robert Storr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Storr_(art_academic) "Robert Storr (art academic)"), mentions that the artist's series "reaches back into a whole series of things in the postwar period-it has a kind of exaltation I have not seen before".[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:0-25) During this Venetian showing, Anatsui wanted to create a new experience for his viewers conceptually. He believes that "human life is not something which is cut and dried. It is something that is constantly in a state of change."[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14) At this point, he began to refer his metalworks as hangings instead of "cloths".[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14)

[![Image 6](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/f/f5/Another_Man%27s_Cloth%2C_2006%2C_El_Anatsui_at_Rubell_DC_2022.jpg/250px-Another_Man%27s_Cloth%2C_2006%2C_El_Anatsui_at_Rubell_DC_2022.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Another_Man's_Cloth,_2006,_El_Anatsui_at_Rubell_DC_2022.jpg)

_Another Man's Cloth_ (2006) at the [Rubell Museum DC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubell_Museum#Rubell_Museum_DC "Rubell Museum") in 2022

A 2010 retrospective of his work, entitled _When I Last Wrote to You About Africa_, was organized by the [Museum for African Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_for_African_Art "Museum for African Art") and opened at the [Royal Ontario Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Ontario_Museum "Royal Ontario Museum") in [Toronto, Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto "Toronto"), Canada. It subsequently toured venues in the United States for three years, concluding at the [University of Michigan Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Michigan_Museum_of_Art "University of Michigan Museum of Art").

A major exhibition of recent works, entitled _Gravity & Grace: Monumental Works by El Anatsui_, had its [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") premiere at the [Brooklyn Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Museum "Brooklyn Museum") in 2013. Organized by the [Akron Art Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akron_Art_Museum "Akron Art Museum") (exhibition: 2012), the exhibition later traveled to the [Des Moines Art Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Des_Moines_Art_Center "Des Moines Art Center") (2013–14) and the [Bass Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bass_Museum "Bass Museum") in Miami (2014).[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-26)

A career-spanning survey of his work, organized by [Okwui Enwezor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okwui_Enwezor "Okwui Enwezor") and [Chika Okeke-Agulu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chika_Okeke-Agulu "Chika Okeke-Agulu"), entitled _Triumphant Scale_ drew record-breaking crowds when it opened in March 2019, at Munich's [Haus der Kunst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haus_der_Kunst "Haus der Kunst"). From there, the show travelled to the [Arab Museum of Modern Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_Museum_of_Modern_Art "Arab Museum of Modern Art"), in Doha, and later to the [Kunstmuseum Bern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kunstmuseum_Bern "Kunstmuseum Bern") in 2020.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-Lucas_40-23)

Anatsui was selected for the 2023 Hyundai Commission at the Turbine Hall at [Tate Modern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tate_Modern "Tate Modern"); a vast display space for large-scale sculptural and site-specific artworks. His work, _Behind the Red Moon_, is made of thousands of metal bottle tops and fragments, building upon his work with materials linked to the transatlantic slave trade, and was on view through 14 April 2024.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-28)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-29)

## Other activities

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Other activities")]

Anatsui was selected to be a member of the International Society for Education through Art (InSEA) world council in 1992 for his work in education.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14) Anatsui was a founding member and fellow of the [Forum for African Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forum_for_African_Arts?action=edit&redlink=1 "Forum for African Arts (page does not exist)") in 2000. That year he also became a member of the International Selection Committee for the [Dakar Biennale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dakar_Biennale "Dakar Biennale") in Senegal.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14) In 2001 he was a fellow at the [Civitella Ranieri Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civitella_Ranieri_Foundation "Civitella Ranieri Foundation") in Italy.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:1-30)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14)

## Recognition

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Recognition")]

### Awards

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Awards")]

Anatsui won an honorable mention at the First [Ghana National Art Competition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghana_National_Art_Competition?action=edit&redlink=1 "Ghana National Art Competition (page does not exist)") as an undergraduate student in 1968. The following year he was awarded the Best Student of the Year at the [College of Art in Kumasi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_of_Art_in_Kumasi?action=edit&redlink=1 "College of Art in Kumasi (page does not exist)"), Ghana.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14) In 1983 he won a commission for two large public sculptures made of terrazzo-surfaced cement on the [Nsukka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nsukka "Nsukka") campus.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14) He was selected to be one of ten artists invited to the [Zweites Symposium Nordesekkuste](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zweites_Symposium_Nordesekkuste?action=edit&redlink=1 "Zweites Symposium Nordesekkuste (page does not exist)") residency in [Cuxhaven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuxhaven "Cuxhaven"), [West Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Germany "West Germany"), in 1984.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14)

In 1990, Anatsui was invited to the 44th annual [Venice Biennale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice_Biennale "Venice Biennale") show _5 Contemporary African Artists_, where he received an honorable mention.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14) That year he was included in the American documentary _Nigerian Art-Kindred Spirits_.

In 2015, the Venice Biennale awarded Anatsui the [Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice_Biennale#Awards "Venice Biennale").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-31)[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-32) In 2017, Anatsui was awarded the [Praemium Imperiale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Praemium_Imperiale "Praemium Imperiale"), the first Ghanaian to win this international art prize.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-33)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-34)

Other awards include:

*   1990 – Public Prize, 7th Annual Triennale der Kleinplastik[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14)
*   1995 – Kansai Telecasting Prize, 6th Osaka Sculpture Triennial[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:1-30)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14)
*   1998 – Bronze Prize, 9th Osaka Sculpture Triennial[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14)
*   2008 – Visionaries! Award, [Museum of Arts and Design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Arts_and_Design "Museum of Arts and Design") (MAD)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14)
*   2009 – [Prince Claus Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Claus_Fund "Prince Claus Fund")
*   2009 – Artist Honoree, 30th Anniversary Celebration, [National Museum of African Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_African_Art "National Museum of African Art")[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14)
*   2016 – Honorary doctorate, [Harvard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University")[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-37)
*   2017 – Honorary doctorate, [Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kwame_Nkrumah_University_of_Science_and_Technology "Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology")[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-38)[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-39)
*   2023 – _[Time 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time\_100 "Time 100")_[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-40)

'''El Anatsui''' ({{IPAc-en|ɛ|l|_|ˌ|æ|n|ə|t|ˈ|s|uː|i}}; born 4 February 1944)<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.meer.com/en/24283-el-anatsui | title=El Anatsui | date=15 March 2017 }}</ref><ref>{{cite encyclopedia | url=https://www.britannica.com/biography/El-Anatsui | title=El Anatsui | Biography, Art, Bottle Caps, & Facts | Britannica | encyclopedia=Encyclopedia Britannica }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.guggenheim-bilbao.eus/en/the-collection/artists/el-anatsui | title=Biografía y obras: Anatsui, el | Guggenheim Museum Bilbao }}</ref> is a Ghanaian [[sculptor]] active for much of his career in Nigeria. He has drawn particular international attention for his "[[Bottle cap|bottle-top]] installations". These installations consist of thousands of [[Aluminium recycling|aluminum pieces sourced]] from alcohol recycling stations and sewn together with copper wire, which are then transformed into metallic cloth-like wall sculptures. Such materials, while seemingly stiff and sturdy, are actually free and flexible, which often helps with manipulation when installing his sculptures.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://art21.org/artist/el-anatsui/|title=El Anatsui|last=Sollins|first=Marybeth|website=Art 21}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Christinee|first=Lindsay|date=8 September 2020|title=Fall In Love With These Sustainable Artists|url=https://thewellnessfeed.com/sustainable-artists-making-art-from-trash-0908/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210122032741/https://thewellnessfeed.com/sustainable-artists-making-art-from-trash-0908/ |archive-date=22 January 2021 |access-date=19 January 2021|website=The Wellness Feed|language=en-US}}</ref>
