**El Anatsui** ([/ɛ l ˌ æ n ə t ˈ s uː i/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); born 4 February 1944)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#)!Image 13[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#)!Image 14[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#) is a Ghanaian !Image 15![Image 16sculptor!Image 17](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sculptor "Sculptor")!Image 18 active for much of his career in Nigeria. He has drawn particular international attention for his "!Image 19![Image 20bottle-top!Image 21](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bottle_cap "Bottle cap")!Image 22 installations". These installations consist of thousands of !Image 23![Image 24aluminum pieces sourced!Image 25](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium_recycling "Aluminium recycling")!Image 26 from alcohol recycling stations and sewn together with copper wire, which are then transformed into metallic cloth-like wall sculptures. Such materials, while seemingly stiff and sturdy, are actually free and flexible, which often helps with manipulation when installing his sculptures.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#)!Image 27[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#)!Image 28

Anatsui was included in the 2023 !Image 29![Image 30_Time_ 100!Image 31](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_100 "Time 100")!Image 32 list of the world's most influential people.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#) In the article, artist and art historian Okeke-Agulu writes, "The breathtaking combination of experimental rigor and inspired vision turns such unassuming materials as printer's plates or liquor-bottle caps into the magnificent constructions and compositions displayed around the world."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#)!Image 33

## Early life and education

El Anatsui was born in !Image 34![Image 35Anyako!Image 36](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anyako "Anyako")!Image 37, in the !Image 38![Image 39Volta Region!Image 40](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volta_Region "Volta Region")!Image 41 of Ghana. The youngest of his father's 32 children, Anatsui lost his mother and was raised by his uncle. His first experience with art was through drawing letters on a chalkboard.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#) His lettering attempts drew the attention of his school's headmaster, who encouraged his effort by providing him with more chalk. Because of his age at the time (just after kindergarten), he regarded the letters more as images than as letters--the forms interested him.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#)!Image 42

Anatsui received his B.A in 1968 from the !Image 43![Image 44College of Art and Built Environment (KNUST)!Image 45](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_of_Art_and_Built_Environment_(KNUST) "College of Art and Built Environment (KNUST)")!Image 46 in Kumasi, Ghana. He received his postgraduate diploma in Art Education the following year, in 1969, from !Image 47![Image 48Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST)!Image 49](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kwame_Nkrumah_University_of_Science_and_Technology "Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology")!Image 50, also in Kumasi.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#)!Image 51

Some of his early artistic influences include !Image 52![Image 53Oku Ampofo!Image 54](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oku_Ampofo "Oku Ampofo")!Image 55, !Image 56![Image 57Vincent Akwete Kofi!Image 58](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_Kofi "Vincent Kofi")!Image 59, and !Image 60![Image 61Kofi Antubam!Image 62](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kofi_Antubam "Kofi Antubam")!Image 63, all of whom began to reject foreign influences in their practices in favor of indigenous art forms.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#) After graduating in 1969, Anatsui assumed a teaching position at Winneba Specialist Training College (now !Image 64![Image 65University of Education!Image 66](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Education,_Winneba "University of Education, Winneba")!Image 67), a role that had previously been filled by Kofi.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#)!Image 68

He began teaching at the !Image 69![Image 70University of Nigeria, Nsukka!Image 71](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria "University of Nigeria")!Image 72 in 1975.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#) He became a senior lecturer for the Fine and Applied Arts department in 1982, and later became head of that department and full professor of sculpture in 1996, a role he occupied until 2011.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#) His presence at the University of Nsukka led to his affiliation with the !Image 73![Image 74Nsukka group!Image 75](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nsukka_group "Nsukka group")!Image 76.

> It has taken many years to find artists who can occupy a prominent place on the global circuit while choosing to reside outside the !Image 77![Image 78metropolitan!Image 79](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_area "Metropolitan area")!Image 80 centres. !Image 81![Image 82William Kentridge!Image 83](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Kentridge "William Kentridge")!Image 84 has made his reputation from !Image 85![Image 86Johannesburg!Image 87](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannesburg "Johannesburg")!Image 88, and El Anatsui has conquered the planet while living and working in the Nigerian university town of Nsukka.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#)!Image 89

## Artwork

Anatsui notes that, through school and in university, "everything we were doing was western," especially within the fine arts department of his university; he felt that there was something missing in his education for its lack of focus on his own culture.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#) In order to rectify this, he started visiting the National Cultural Centre of Ghana, also in Kumasi, to engage with the musicians, graphic artists, textile artists, printers, and creative artists of all types. It was there that he encountered !Image 90![Image 91Adinkra!Image 92](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adinkra_symbols "Adinkra symbols")!Image 93, a system of signs and symbols, which was his first introduction to abstract art and opened up a new world of artistic possibilities for him.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#)!Image 94

In the 1970s, Anatsui worked frequently in wood. He was particularly interested in wooden trays, which he often saw used in the markets to display food items and other wares--he would carve them or engrave them with Adinkra symbols and other marks using hot rods.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#) He also began using wood to construct wall panels from strips placed next to each other, the surface decorated with designs imparted on the material through the use of chain saws, gouges, flame, or paint.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#) In the late 70s, he began working in clay: pots, in particular, exploring themes of fragility and dilapidation. He was interested in how, even after a pot breaks and ceases being used in the way we commonly think (for food, water), it takes on a new purpose, even acquires more uses, from the mundane to the spiritual. Most intriguing to him is the use of pot shards for presenting offerings. He said, "It's as if the pot, having broken, is transformed into a dimension which makes it ideal for use by ancestors and deities who are themselves in the spirit dimension."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#)!Image 95

After his work with the broken pots, Anatsui explored food-adjacent themes in other materials: wood, again, in the form of mortars; equipment used to process !Image 96![Image 97cassava!Image 98](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassava "Cassava")!Image 99, and bottle tops.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#)!Image 100

Much of Anatsui's work features found materials, or materials that had a life of use prior to being formed into this artworks. His emphasis on the found object, however, is less !Image 101![Image 102Duchampian!Image 103](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcel_Duchamp "Marcel Duchamp")!Image 104, and more focused on the history of use and the evidence of the human hand in the material.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#)!Image 105

> "When something has been used, there is a certain charge, a certain energy, that has to do with the people who have touched it and used it and sometimes abused it. This helps to direct what one is doing, and also to root what one is doing in the environment and the culture."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#)!Image 106

Metal bottle caps are a favorite material of his; like cloth, Anatsui describes, an arrangement of bottle caps is versatile, allowing him to consider his art both sculpturally (through the form of the caps) and in a painterly manner (through the colors of the caps). Further, he appreciates the glimpse that bottle caps give into current and historical political and sociological issues, by virtue of the names and colors of various drink brands that are printed onto the caps.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#)!Image 107

> "The most important thing for me is the transformation. The fact that these media, each identifying a brand of drink, are no longer going back to serve the same role but are elements that could generate some reflection, some thinking, or just some wonder. This is possible because they are removed from their accustomed, functional context into a new one, and they bring along their histories and identities."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#)!Image 108

A number of themes are present in Anatsui's work: the destruction and subsequent reconstitution of material as a metaphor for life and the changes Africa faced under colonialism and since independence; traditional themes and motifs of West African strip woven cloth and other !Image 109![Image 110African textiles!Image 111](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_textiles "African textiles")!Image 112; and concern over Western scholarly misinterpretation of African history and the distortions it has caused.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#) His work is also thematically connected to the West African cultural landscape and ideas of consumption and labor.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#)!Image 113

The idea of !Image 114![Image 115Sankofa!Image 116](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sankofa "Sankofa")!Image 117 [translated as "go back and retrieve"] is also present in Anatsui's work. He views it as a way of drawing on the past, the lessons it offers, to chart a mode of moving forward. For him, Sankofa described a need to draw from what was immediately around him; Ghana became independent when he was in high school, and much of his education had been focused on western art and art history, and so he felt called to 'go back and retrieve' aspects of Ghanaian culture that had been suppressed, something he described as a sort of "quest for self-discovery."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#)!Image 118

## Exhibitions

[![Image 119](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8f/El_Anatsui_-_Man%27s_Cloth.jpg/250px-El_Anatsui_-_Man%27s_Cloth.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:El_Anatsui_-_Man's_Cloth.jpg)

_Man's Cloth_ (1998–2001) at the !Image 120![Image 121British Museum!Image 122](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Museum "British Museum")!Image 123 in 2009

Anatsui's career grew gradually, starting in his home village of !Image 124![Image 125Nsukka!Image 126](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nsukka "Nsukka")!Image 127 before branching off to places such as !Image 128![Image 129Enugu!Image 130](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enugu_(city) "Enugu (city)")!Image 131 and !Image 132![Image 133Lagos!Image 134](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagos "Lagos")!Image 135, and eventually internationally.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#) In 1990, Anatsui had his first important group show at the !Image 136![Image 137Studio Museum!Image 138](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studio_Museum_in_Harlem "Studio Museum in Harlem")!Image 139 In !Image 140![Image 141Harlem!Image 142](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harlem "Harlem")!Image 143, !Image 144![Image 145New York!Image 146](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)")!Image 147. He also was one of three artists singled out in the 1990 exhibition "Contemporary African Artists: Changing Traditions", which was extended for five years.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#)↵Anatsui has since exhibited his work around the world, including at the !Image 148![Image 149Brooklyn Museum!Image 150](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Museum "Brooklyn Museum")!Image 151 (2013);[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#) the !Image 152![Image 153Clark Art Institute!Image 154](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clark_Art_Institute "Clark Art Institute")!Image 155 (2011);[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#) the Rice University Art Gallery, Houston (2010);[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#) the !Image 156![Image 157Metropolitan Museum of Art!Image 158](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Museum_of_Art "Metropolitan Museum of Art")!Image 159, New York (2008–09);[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#) the !Image 160![Image 161National Museum of African Art!Image 162](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_African_Art "National Museum of African Art")!Image 163, Smithsonian Institution, Washington, D.C. (2008);[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#) the !Image 164![Image 165Fowler Museum at UCLA!Image 166](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fowler_Museum_at_UCLA "Fowler Museum at UCLA")!Image 167 (2007);[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#) the !Image 168![Image 169Venice Biennale!Image 170](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice_Biennale "Venice Biennale")!Image 171 (1990 and 2007);[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#) the !Image 172![Image 173Hayward Gallery!Image 174](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hayward_Gallery "Hayward Gallery")!Image 175 (2005);[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#) the !Image 176![Image 177Liverpool Biennial!Image 178](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool_Biennial "Liverpool Biennial")!Image 179 (2002);[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#) the National Museum of African Art (2001);[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#) the !Image 180![Image 181Centre de Cultura Contemporània de Barcelona!Image 182](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centre_de_Cultura_Contempor%C3%A0nia_de_Barcelona "Centre de Cultura Contemporània de Barcelona")!Image 183 (2001);[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#) the 8th Osaka Sculpture Triennale (1995);[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#) the 5th !Image 184![Image 185Gwangju Biennale!Image 186](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gwangju_Biennale "Gwangju Biennale")!Image 187 (2004); the !Image 188![Image 189Arab Museum of Modern Art!Image 190](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_Museum_of_Modern_Art "Arab Museum of Modern Art")!Image 191 in Doha (2019);[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#) and the !Image 192![Image 193Kunstmuseum Bern!Image 194](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kunstmuseum_Bern "Kunstmuseum Bern")!Image 195 (2020).[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#)↵In 1995, Anatsui held his first solo exhibition outside of Africa in !Image 196![Image 197London!Image 198](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London")!Image 199. He expressed a variety of themes and demonstrated how African art can be shown in a multitude of ways that are not seen as "typical" African.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#) His work utilized conceptual modes used by European and American artists but hardly in African countries.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#) Anatsui showed his work at the de Young Museum in !Image 200![Image 201San Francisco!Image 202](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco")!Image 203 in 2005. This was his first time "appear[ing] as part of the permanent collection in a major art museum".[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#) Also in 2005, his exhibition at New York's !Image 204![Image 205Skoto Gallery!Image 206](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skoto_Gallery "Skoto Gallery")!Image 207, _Danudo_, was the first display of his metal sheets in an American city.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#) At this gallery, Skoto Aghahowa presented Anatsui's wood wall panels alongside !Image 208![Image 209Sol LeWitt!Image 210](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sol_LeWitt "Sol LeWitt")!Image 211's drawings. This exhibition popularized his bottle-cap works as he gained more recognition in the press.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#)!Image 212

[![Image 213](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/68/Artempo_ElAnatsui.jpg/250px-Artempo_ElAnatsui.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Artempo_ElAnatsui.jpg)

Anatsui's !Image 214![Image 215Palazzo Fortuny!Image 216](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Fortuny "Palazzo Fortuny")!Image 217 Artempo exhibition in 2007

Anatsui was invited to the !Image 218![Image 219Venice Biennale!Image 220](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice_Biennale "Venice Biennale")!Image 221 in 2006 and again in 2007 where he was commissioned to make two hanging metal tapestries. During the 2007 edition, he exhibited his works at the !Image 222![Image 223Palazzo Fortuny!Image 224](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Fortuny "Palazzo Fortuny")!Image 225 which consisted of newly built walls for him to display three metal hangings entitled _Dusasa_.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#) Each artwork demonstrated different textures and colors including golds, reds, and blacks. The way the bottle tops draped throughout the hangings created a sense of gentleness that made it stand apart from the other works in the gallery.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#) The art curator of the Biennale, !Image 226![Image 227Robert Storr!Image 228](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Storr_(art_academic) "Robert Storr (art academic)")!Image 229, mentions that the artist's series "reaches back into a whole series of things in the postwar period-it has a kind of exaltation I have not seen before".[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#) During this Venetian showing, Anatsui wanted to create a new experience for his viewers conceptually. He believes that "human life is not something which is cut and dried. It is something that is constantly in a state of change."[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#) At this point, he began to refer his metalworks as hangings instead of "cloths".[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#)!Image 230

'''El Anatsui''' ({{IPAc-en|ɛ|l|_|ˌ|æ|n|ə|t|ˈ|s|uː|i}}; born 4 February 1944)<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.meer.com/en/24283-el-anatsui | title=El Anatsui | date=15 March 2017 }}</ref><ref>{{cite encyclopedia | url=https://www.britannica.com/biography/El-Anatsui | title=El Anatsui | Biography, Art, Bottle Caps, & Facts | Britannica | encyclopedia=Encyclopedia Britannica }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.guggenheim-bilbao.eus/en/the-collection/artists/el-anatsui | title=Biografía y obras: Anatsui, el | Guggenheim Museum Bilbao }}</ref> is a Ghanaian [[sculptor]] active for much of his career in Nigeria. He has drawn particular international attention for his "[[Bottle cap|bottle-top]] installations". These installations consist of thousands of [[Aluminium recycling|aluminum pieces sourced]] from alcohol recycling stations and sewn together with copper wire, which are then transformed into metallic cloth-like wall sculptures. Such materials, while seemingly stiff and sturdy, are actually free and flexible, which often helps with manipulation when installing his sculptures.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://art21.org/artist/el-anatsui/|title=El Anatsui|last=Sollins|first=Marybeth|website=Art 21}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last=Christinee|first=Lindsay|date=8 September 2020|title=Fall In Love With These Sustainable Artists|url=https://thewellnessfeed.com/sustainable-artists-making-art-from-trash-0908/|url-status=live|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210122032741/https://thewellnessfeed.com/sustainable-artists-making-art-from-trash-0908/ |archive-date=22 January 2021 |access-date=19 January 2021|website=The Wellness Feed|language=en-US}}</ref>

**El Anatsui** ([/ɛ l ˌ æ n ə t ˈ s uː i/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); born 4 February 1944)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#)!Image 13[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#)!Image 14[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#) is a Ghanaian !Image 15![Image 16sculptor!Image 17](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sculptor "Sculptor")!Image 18 active for much of his career in Nigeria. He has drawn particular international attention for his "!Image 19![Image 20bottle-top!Image 21](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bottle_cap "Bottle cap")!Image 22 installations". These installations consist of thousands of !Image 23![Image 24aluminum pieces sourced!Image 25](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium_recycling "Aluminium recycling")!Image 26 from alcohol recycling stations and sewn together with copper wire, which are then transformed into metallic cloth-like wall sculptures. Such materials, while seemingly stiff and sturdy, are actually free and flexible, which often helps with manipulation when installing his sculptures.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#)!Image 27[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#)!Image 28

Anatsui was included in the 2023 !Image 29![Image 30_Time_ 100!Image 31](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_100 "Time 100")!Image 32 list of the world's most influential people.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#) In the article, artist and art historian Okeke-Agulu writes, "The breathtaking combination of experimental rigor and inspired vision turns such unassuming materials as printer's plates or liquor-bottle caps into the magnificent constructions and compositions displayed around the world."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#)!Image 33

## Early life and education

El Anatsui was born in !Image 34![Image 35Anyako!Image 36](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anyako "Anyako")!Image 37, in the !Image 38![Image 39Volta Region!Image 40](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volta_Region "Volta Region")!Image 41 of Ghana. The youngest of his father's 32 children, Anatsui lost his mother and was raised by his uncle. His first experience with art was through drawing letters on a chalkboard.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#) His lettering attempts drew the attention of his school's headmaster, who encouraged his effort by providing him with more chalk. Because of his age at the time (just after kindergarten), he regarded the letters more as images than as letters--the forms interested him.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#)!Image 42

Anatsui received his B.A in 1968 from the !Image 43![Image 44College of Art and Built Environment (KNUST)!Image 45](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_of_Art_and_Built_Environment_(KNUST) "College of Art and Built Environment (KNUST)")!Image 46 in Kumasi, Ghana. He received his postgraduate diploma in Art Education the following year, in 1969, from !Image 47![Image 48Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST)!Image 49](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kwame_Nkrumah_University_of_Science_and_Technology "Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology")!Image 50, also in Kumasi.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#)!Image 51

Some of his early artistic influences include !Image 52![Image 53Oku Ampofo!Image 54](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oku_Ampofo "Oku Ampofo")!Image 55, !Image 56![Image 57Vincent Akwete Kofi!Image 58](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_Kofi "Vincent Kofi")!Image 59, and !Image 60![Image 61Kofi Antubam!Image 62](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kofi_Antubam "Kofi Antubam")!Image 63, all of whom began to reject foreign influences in their practices in favor of indigenous art forms.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#) After graduating in 1969, Anatsui assumed a teaching position at Winneba Specialist Training College (now !Image 64![Image 65University of Education!Image 66](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Education,_Winneba "University of Education, Winneba")!Image 67), a role that had previously been filled by Kofi.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#)!Image 68

He began teaching at the !Image 69![Image 70University of Nigeria, Nsukka!Image 71](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria "University of Nigeria")!Image 72 in 1975.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#) He became a senior lecturer for the Fine and Applied Arts department in 1982, and later became head of that department and full professor of sculpture in 1996, a role he occupied until 2011.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#) His presence at the University of Nsukka led to his affiliation with the !Image 73![Image 74Nsukka group!Image 75](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nsukka_group "Nsukka group")!Image 76.

> It has taken many years to find artists who can occupy a prominent place on the global circuit while choosing to reside outside the !Image 77![Image 78metropolitan!Image 79](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_area "Metropolitan area")!Image 80 centres. !Image 81![Image 82William Kentridge!Image 83](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Kentridge "William Kentridge")!Image 84 has made his reputation from !Image 85![Image 86Johannesburg!Image 87](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannesburg "Johannesburg")!Image 88, and El Anatsui has conquered the planet while living and working in the Nigerian university town of Nsukka.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#)!Image 89

## Artwork

Anatsui notes that, through school and in university, "everything we were doing was western," especially within the fine arts department of his university; he felt that there was something missing in his education for its lack of focus on his own culture.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#) In order to rectify this, he started visiting the National Cultural Centre of Ghana, also in Kumasi, to engage with the musicians, graphic artists, textile artists, printers, and creative artists of all types. It was there that he encountered !Image 90![Image 91Adinkra!Image 92](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adinkra_symbols "Adinkra symbols")!Image 93, a system of signs and symbols, which was his first introduction to abstract art and opened up a new world of artistic possibilities for him.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#)!Image 94

In the 1970s, Anatsui worked frequently in wood. He was particularly interested in wooden trays, which he often saw used in the markets to display food items and other wares--he would carve them or engrave them with Adinkra symbols and other marks using hot rods.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#) He also began using wood to construct wall panels from strips placed next to each other, the surface decorated with designs imparted on the material through the use of chain saws, gouges, flame, or paint.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#) In the late 70s, he began working in clay: pots, in particular, exploring themes of fragility and dilapidation. He was interested in how, even after a pot breaks and ceases being used in the way we commonly think (for food, water), it takes on a new purpose, even acquires more uses, from the mundane to the spiritual. Most intriguing to him is the use of pot shards for presenting offerings. He said, "It's as if the pot, having broken, is transformed into a dimension which makes it ideal for use by ancestors and deities who are themselves in the spirit dimension."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#)!Image 95

After his work with the broken pots, Anatsui explored food-adjacent themes in other materials: wood, again, in the form of mortars; equipment used to process !Image 96![Image 97cassava!Image 98](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassava "Cassava")!Image 99, and bottle tops.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#)!Image 100

Much of Anatsui's work features found materials, or materials that had a life of use prior to being formed into this artworks. His emphasis on the found object, however, is less !Image 101![Image 102Duchampian!Image 103](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcel_Duchamp "Marcel Duchamp")!Image 104, and more focused on the history of use and the evidence of the human hand in the material.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#)!Image 105

> "When something has been used, there is a certain charge, a certain energy, that has to do with the people who have touched it and used it and sometimes abused it. This helps to direct what one is doing, and also to root what one is doing in the environment and the culture."[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#)!Image 106

Metal bottle caps are a favorite material of his; like cloth, Anatsui describes, an arrangement of bottle caps is versatile, allowing him to consider his art both sculpturally (through the form of the caps) and in a painterly manner (through the colors of the caps). Further, he appreciates the glimpse that bottle caps give into current and historical political and sociological issues, by virtue of the names and colors of various drink brands that are printed onto the caps.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#)!Image 107

> "The most important thing for me is the transformation. The fact that these media, each identifying a brand of drink, are no longer going back to serve the same role but are elements that could generate some reflection, some thinking, or just some wonder. This is possible because they are removed from their accustomed, functional context into a new one, and they bring along their histories and identities."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#)!Image 108

A number of themes are present in Anatsui's work: the destruction and subsequent reconstitution of material as a metaphor for life and the changes Africa faced under colonialism and since independence; traditional themes and motifs of West African strip woven cloth and other !Image 109![Image 110African textiles!Image 111](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_textiles "African textiles")!Image 112; and concern over Western scholarly misinterpretation of African history and the distortions it has caused.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#) His work is also thematically connected to the West African cultural landscape and ideas of consumption and labor.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#)!Image 113

The idea of !Image 114![Image 115Sankofa!Image 116](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sankofa "Sankofa")!Image 117 [translated as "go back and retrieve"] is also present in Anatsui's work. He views it as a way of drawing on the past, the lessons it offers, to chart a mode of moving forward. For him, Sankofa described a need to draw from what was immediately around him; Ghana became independent when he was in high school, and much of his education had been focused on western art and art history, and so he felt called to 'go back and retrieve' aspects of Ghanaian culture that had been suppressed, something he described as a sort of "quest for self-discovery."[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit#)!Image 118

## Exhibitions

The **University of Nigeria, Nsukka** (**UNN**) is a [public](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_university "Public university")[land-grant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land-grant_university "Land-grant university")[research university](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university "Research university") in [Nsukka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nsukka "Nsukka"), Enugu State, Nigeria. Founded in 1955 by President [Nnamdi Azikiwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nnamdi_Azikiwe "Nnamdi Azikiwe"), the university was formally opened on 7 October 1960. It was one of the [first generation universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Education_in_Nigeria#First_generation_universities "Education in Nigeria") in Nigeria.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-7) The university has campuses in Nsukka (its main campus), [Enugu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enugu_(city) "Enugu (city)"), and Ituku-Ozalla, all in Enugu State, and in [Aba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aba,_Nigeria "Aba, Nigeria"), [Abia State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abia_State "Abia State").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-8)

The University of Nigeria is the first indigenous and autonomous university in Nigeria. It is modelled after the [American educational system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_educational_system "American educational system"). It was the first [land-grant university](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land-grant_university "Land-grant university") in [Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa "Africa") and one of the five most reputed [universities in Nigeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universities_in_Nigeria "Universities in Nigeria"). The university has seventeen (17) Faculties and 102 [academic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_degree "Academic degree") departments, offering over 108 undergraduate programmes and 211 postgraduate programmes.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-9)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Nigeria&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

A law to establish a university in the [Eastern Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Region,_Nigeria "Eastern Region, Nigeria") of Nigeria was passed on 18 May 1955.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-10) Advice was sought from educationists in the UK and the US to help in the planning of the physical and educational aspects of the proposed university.

Under the joint auspices of the [Inter-University Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inter-University_Council_for_East_Africa "Inter-University Council for East Africa") for [Higher Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higher_education "Higher education") and Overseas and the International Co-operation Administration (now the [United States Agency for International Development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Agency_for_International_Development "United States Agency for International Development")), J.W. Cook, vice-chancellor of the [University of Exeter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Exeter "University of Exeter"), [John A. Hannah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_A._Hannah "John A. Hannah"), President of [Michigan State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_State_University "Michigan State University") and [Glen L. Taggart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glen_L._Taggart "Glen L. Taggart"), Dean of International Programs at Michigan State University, came to Nigeria in 1958. The team surveyed the site in Nsukka and extensively investigated a great variety of factors pertinent to the establishment of a new university.

The results of their efforts were contained in a [white paper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_paper "White paper") issued by the Eastern Nigeria Government on 30 November 1958. They had recommended, "that the development of the University of Nigeria based upon the concept of service to problems and needs of Nigeria, is a desirable project and one that should receive support from any source which could help to make it a sound endeavour".

They further recommended that a provisional council be established to "draw upon the technical and consultative resources available throughout the world for help in planning the institution".

The provisional council, authorized by the Eastern Nigeria Legislature, was appointed by the Governor in Council in April 1959, and given the necessary financial and administrative powers to build a sound university. It reflected the spirit of international co-operation which has given birth to the institution. It consisted of [Dr. Nnamdi Azikiwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dr._Nnamdi_Azikiwe "Dr. Nnamdi Azikiwe"), chairman, Dr [T. Olawale Elias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taslim_Olawale_Elias "Taslim Olawale Elias") and Dr [Okechukwu Ikejiani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okechukwu_Ikejiani "Okechukwu Ikejiani") from the Federation of Nigeria, [J. S. Fulton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._S._Fulton "J. S. Fulton") from the United Kingdom, Dr. Marguerite Cartwright and Dr. Eldon Lee Johnson from the United States. The university was formally opened on 7 October 1960, as the climax to the Nigerian independence celebrations in the country's Eastern Region, by [Princess Alexandra of Kent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princess_Alexandra_of_Kent "Princess Alexandra of Kent"). Classes began on 17 October 1960 with an enrollment of 220 students and 13 members of the academic staff. The opening convocation addresses were delivered by the Chairman of the Provisional Council, [Nnamdi Azikiwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nnamdi_Azikiwe "Nnamdi Azikiwe"), the first President of the Federation of Nigeria, and by [John A. Hannah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_A._Hannah "John A. Hannah"), president of [Michigan State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_State_University "Michigan State University").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The university was fully [autonomous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autonomous "Autonomous"), with the power to grant its own degrees. Technically speaking, therefore, it became the first fully-fledged university in Nigeria, since [Ibadan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibadan "Ibadan") was still at that time a university college granting London degrees. It also became the first university established by a Nigerian Regional Government. [The University College Ibadan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Ibadan "University of Ibadan"), the oldest degree-awarding institution, cut its umbilical cord with [London in January 1963](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"), becoming the University of Ibadan. In July 1967, it turned out the first graduates holding Ibadan (rather than London) [degrees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_degree "Academic degree"),[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-11) by which time Nsukka had produced two crops of graduates and taken all the [publicity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publicity "Publicity") for turning out the first [graduates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graduation "Graduation") of an autonomous Nigerian university.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-12)

## Campuses

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Nigeria&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Campuses")]

[![Image 6: University of Nigeria Enugu Campus](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a6/University_of_Nigeria_Enugu_Campus.jpg/250px-University_of_Nigeria_Enugu_Campus.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:University_of_Nigeria_Enugu_Campus.jpg)

**University of Nigeria Enugu Campus**

**The university has four campuses:**

1. the main campus in Nsukka;

2. Enugu campus, popular with the acronym "UNEC" (University of Nigeria, Enugu Campus);

3. Ituku Ozalla campus, known as UNTH (University of Nigeria Teaching Hospital) Ituku Ozalla;

4. [Aba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aba,_Abia "Aba, Abia") campus, with the acronym "UNAC" (University of Nigeria, Aba Campus).

The main campus of the university is located on 871 hectares of hilly [savannah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savanna "Savanna") in the town of Nsukka, about eighty [kilometres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilometres_per_hour "Kilometres per hour") north of Enugu, and enjoys a very pleasant and healthy climate. Additionally 209 [hectares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hectare "Hectare") of arable land are available for an [experimental agricultural farm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experiment "Experiment") and 207 hectares for staff housing development. There is regular road transport between Nsukka and Enugu, and Nsukka is also quite easily accessible from all parts of Nigeria. There are modern shopping facilities and a large market in Nsukka town.

The Nsukka campus houses the [Faculties of Agriculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agriculture "Agriculture"), [Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arts "Arts"), [Biological Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biological_Sciences "Biological Sciences"), [Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Education "Education"), [Engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engineering_education "Engineering education"), [Pharmaceutical Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pharmaceutical_Sciences "Pharmaceutical Sciences"), [Physical Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physical_Sciences "Physical Sciences"), [Social Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_science "Social science"), Vocational Technical Education, and [Veterinary Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veterinary_medicine "Veterinary medicine").

The former Nigerian [College of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_of_Arts_and_Sciences "College of Arts and Sciences"), [Science and Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_and_Technology "Science and Technology"), Enugu, was incorporated into the university in 1961, and its buildings now form the Enugu Campus [(200 hectares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hectare "Hectare")) of the university located in the heart of Enugu, the administrative capital of Enugu State of Nigeria. Enugu is a modern city, accessible by air, rail and road. [The Faculties of Business Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Business_administration "Business administration"), [Environmental Studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental_studies "Environmental studies"), [Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law "Law"), Basic Medical Sciences, and [Health Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_Sciences "Health Sciences") are located at the Enugu Campus.

The teaching hospital attached to the university is presently sited at Ituku-Ozalla (25 kilometres south of Enugu) on a 500-hectare (1,200-acre) site. It also hosts the [Faculty of Dentistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faculty_of_Dentistry "Faculty of Dentistry")/[Dental Surgery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dental_surgery "Dental surgery") and [Medical Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sciences "Medical sciences").

The Aba campus (UNAC) hosts the National Institute for Nigerian Languages.

A former campus was opened in October 1973 in [Calabar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calabar "Calabar"), [Cross River State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_River_State "Cross River State"). The campus at Calabar became a full-fledged [University of Calabar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Calabar "University of Calabar") in October 1975.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-13)

The official name of the university is the University of Nigeria[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-14) and the official acronym is UNN. "[UN"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations") stands for University of Nigeria while the last "N" stands for Nsukka. This acronym is also shared by the main campus of the university, Nsukka (University of Nigeria, Nsukka). Thus technically, the name University of Nigeria, Nsukka refers to the main campus at Nsukka only while the name University of Nigeria refers to all the campuses of the university. References may be made to the location of the other campuses by mentioning the names of the cities where they are situated rather than a blanket description with the name Nsukka. Students at the Enugu Campus prefer to write the name of their school as University of Nigeria Enugu Campus (UNEC)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-15) if they must add the location of their school. Students from other campuses of the school also prefer same. Official documents of the school describes the school as simply University of Nigeria. They also make this dichotomy when referring to different campuses of the school.

## Academics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Nigeria&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Academics")]

Novelist [Chinua Achebe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinua_Achebe "Chinua Achebe") held research and teaching appointments at the university, beginning in the early 1970s. He worked in the faculty of arts with critic and [African literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_literature "African literature") scholar [Donatus Nwoga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donatus_Nwoga "Donatus Nwoga").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-34) Astrophysicist [Sam Okoye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Ejikeme_Okoye "Samuel Ejikeme Okoye") founded the Space Research Center in 1972. The Centre for Basic Space Research remains one of the few institutions in Africa that carries out research and offers courses in astronomy at both the undergraduate and postgraduate levels.

The first open heart surgical operation in Nigeria and [sub-Saharan Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sub-Saharan_Africa "Sub-Saharan Africa") was undertaken in 1974 at the University of Nigeria Teaching Hospital (UNTH) Enugu. The team was led by visiting [Magdi Yacoub](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magdi_Yacoub "Magdi Yacoub") from the UK and others in the team included Professors [Fabian Udekwu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabian_Udekwu "Fabian Udekwu") and Anyanwu. The College of Medicine has since evolved into the centre for cardiothoracic surgery and tropical cardiology excellence for the West Africa region with the siting of the National Cardiothoracic Center at UNTH Enugu. Much medical research is also being carried out in the college.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-35)

The Department of Fine and Applied Arts is known for the [Nsukka group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nsukka_group "Nsukka group") – seven artists associated with a system of traditional [Igbo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Igbo_people "Igbo people") designs and styles known as _[uli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uli\_(design) "Uli (design)")_.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-37)

The Law Faculty of the university is the oldest in Nigeria; it was established in 1960.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-38)

The Department of Electronic Engineering was named a Center of Excellence in Electronics by the Federal Government of Nigeria in 1982. The department was established in 1981 under the faculty of engineering after the previous department of electronic engineering was split into two separate department.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-39) The department offers a Bachelor of Engineering degree in Electronic Engineering to undergraduates, as well a MSC and Doctoral degree program in relevant specializations under Electronic Engineering. The Department has produced the highest number of first-class graduate than any other department in the university. The department has also produced many overall best graduating students more than any department in the university. It has produced overall university best for the three consecutive academic session in 1995/1996 1996/1997 1997/1998.

### Library

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Nigeria&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Library")]

The University of Nigeria, Nsukka Libraries consist of the Nnamdi Azikiwe Library, the Enugu Campus Main Library and the Medical Library located at the College of Medicine, University of Nigeria Teaching Hospital, Ituku-Ozalla. On 8 March 2009, the multi-complex [Nnamdi Azikiwe Library of University of Nigeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nnamdi_Azikiwe_Library "Nnamdi Azikiwe Library"), Nsukka was officially opened by the then minister of Education, Dr [Sam Egwu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Egwu "Sam Egwu").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-Eke-2014-40) The library has embraced information technology to provide an effective library service to users and this was why it was one of the three leading academic libraries in Nigeria where [TINLIB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tinlib "Tinlib") software was introduced in the 90s.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-41) After so many failed attempts to [automate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automation "Automation") the library using a well robust integrated library management software, the library finally settled for [KOHA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koha_(software) "Koha (software)") Integrated library management software to automate its activities.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-42) The library collection is unique because it contains an [Africana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africana_(artifacts) "Africana (artifacts)") section that houses rare books such as Biafrana and Achebeana. It has a total holding of 350,000 book titles and about 5000 serials titles.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-Eke-2014-40)

The **University of Nigeria, Nsukka** (**UNN**) is a [public](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Public_university "Public university")[land-grant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land-grant_university "Land-grant university")[research university](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university "Research university") in [Nsukka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nsukka "Nsukka"), Enugu State, Nigeria. Founded in 1955 by President [Nnamdi Azikiwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nnamdi_Azikiwe "Nnamdi Azikiwe"), the university was formally opened on 7 October 1960. It was one of the [first generation universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Education_in_Nigeria#First_generation_universities "Education in Nigeria") in Nigeria.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-7) The university has campuses in Nsukka (its main campus), [Enugu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enugu_(city) "Enugu (city)"), and Ituku-Ozalla, all in Enugu State, and in [Aba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aba,_Nigeria "Aba, Nigeria"), [Abia State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abia_State "Abia State").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-8)

The University of Nigeria is the first indigenous and autonomous university in Nigeria. It is modelled after the [American educational system](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_educational_system "American educational system"). It was the first [land-grant university](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land-grant_university "Land-grant university") in [Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa "Africa") and one of the five most reputed [universities in Nigeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Universities_in_Nigeria "Universities in Nigeria"). The university has seventeen (17) Faculties and 102 [academic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_degree "Academic degree") departments, offering over 108 undergraduate programmes and 211 postgraduate programmes.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-9)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Nigeria&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: History")]

A law to establish a university in the [Eastern Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eastern_Region,_Nigeria "Eastern Region, Nigeria") of Nigeria was passed on 18 May 1955.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-10) Advice was sought from educationists in the UK and the US to help in the planning of the physical and educational aspects of the proposed university.

Under the joint auspices of the [Inter-University Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inter-University_Council_for_East_Africa "Inter-University Council for East Africa") for [Higher Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higher_education "Higher education") and Overseas and the International Co-operation Administration (now the [United States Agency for International Development](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_Agency_for_International_Development "United States Agency for International Development")), J.W. Cook, vice-chancellor of the [University of Exeter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Exeter "University of Exeter"), [John A. Hannah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_A._Hannah "John A. Hannah"), President of [Michigan State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_State_University "Michigan State University") and [Glen L. Taggart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glen_L._Taggart "Glen L. Taggart"), Dean of International Programs at Michigan State University, came to Nigeria in 1958. The team surveyed the site in Nsukka and extensively investigated a great variety of factors pertinent to the establishment of a new university.

The results of their efforts were contained in a [white paper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_paper "White paper") issued by the Eastern Nigeria Government on 30 November 1958. They had recommended, "that the development of the University of Nigeria based upon the concept of service to problems and needs of Nigeria, is a desirable project and one that should receive support from any source which could help to make it a sound endeavour".

They further recommended that a provisional council be established to "draw upon the technical and consultative resources available throughout the world for help in planning the institution".

The provisional council, authorized by the Eastern Nigeria Legislature, was appointed by the Governor in Council in April 1959, and given the necessary financial and administrative powers to build a sound university. It reflected the spirit of international co-operation which has given birth to the institution. It consisted of [Dr. Nnamdi Azikiwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dr._Nnamdi_Azikiwe "Dr. Nnamdi Azikiwe"), chairman, Dr [T. Olawale Elias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taslim_Olawale_Elias "Taslim Olawale Elias") and Dr [Okechukwu Ikejiani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okechukwu_Ikejiani "Okechukwu Ikejiani") from the Federation of Nigeria, [J. S. Fulton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._S._Fulton "J. S. Fulton") from the United Kingdom, Dr. Marguerite Cartwright and Dr. Eldon Lee Johnson from the United States. The university was formally opened on 7 October 1960, as the climax to the Nigerian independence celebrations in the country's Eastern Region, by [Princess Alexandra of Kent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princess_Alexandra_of_Kent "Princess Alexandra of Kent"). Classes began on 17 October 1960 with an enrollment of 220 students and 13 members of the academic staff. The opening convocation addresses were delivered by the Chairman of the Provisional Council, [Nnamdi Azikiwe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nnamdi_Azikiwe "Nnamdi Azikiwe"), the first President of the Federation of Nigeria, and by [John A. Hannah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_A._Hannah "John A. Hannah"), president of [Michigan State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michigan_State_University "Michigan State University").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

The university was fully [autonomous](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autonomous "Autonomous"), with the power to grant its own degrees. Technically speaking, therefore, it became the first fully-fledged university in Nigeria, since [Ibadan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ibadan "Ibadan") was still at that time a university college granting London degrees. It also became the first university established by a Nigerian Regional Government. [The University College Ibadan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Ibadan "University of Ibadan"), the oldest degree-awarding institution, cut its umbilical cord with [London in January 1963](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"), becoming the University of Ibadan. In July 1967, it turned out the first graduates holding Ibadan (rather than London) [degrees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academic_degree "Academic degree"),[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-11) by which time Nsukka had produced two crops of graduates and taken all the [publicity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Publicity "Publicity") for turning out the first [graduates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Graduation "Graduation") of an autonomous Nigerian university.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-12)

## Campuses

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Nigeria&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Campuses")]

[![Image 6: University of Nigeria Enugu Campus](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/a6/University_of_Nigeria_Enugu_Campus.jpg/250px-University_of_Nigeria_Enugu_Campus.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:University_of_Nigeria_Enugu_Campus.jpg)

**University of Nigeria Enugu Campus**

**The university has four campuses:**

1. the main campus in Nsukka;

2. Enugu campus, popular with the acronym "UNEC" (University of Nigeria, Enugu Campus);

3. Ituku Ozalla campus, known as UNTH (University of Nigeria Teaching Hospital) Ituku Ozalla;

4. [Aba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aba,_Abia "Aba, Abia") campus, with the acronym "UNAC" (University of Nigeria, Aba Campus).

The main campus of the university is located on 871 hectares of hilly [savannah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Savanna "Savanna") in the town of Nsukka, about eighty [kilometres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kilometres_per_hour "Kilometres per hour") north of Enugu, and enjoys a very pleasant and healthy climate. Additionally 209 [hectares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hectare "Hectare") of arable land are available for an [experimental agricultural farm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Experiment "Experiment") and 207 hectares for staff housing development. There is regular road transport between Nsukka and Enugu, and Nsukka is also quite easily accessible from all parts of Nigeria. There are modern shopping facilities and a large market in Nsukka town.

The Nsukka campus houses the [Faculties of Agriculture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Agriculture "Agriculture"), [Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arts "Arts"), [Biological Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Biological_Sciences "Biological Sciences"), [Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Education "Education"), [Engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engineering_education "Engineering education"), [Pharmaceutical Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pharmaceutical_Sciences "Pharmaceutical Sciences"), [Physical Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Physical_Sciences "Physical Sciences"), [Social Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_science "Social science"), Vocational Technical Education, and [Veterinary Medicine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Veterinary_medicine "Veterinary medicine").

The former Nigerian [College of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_of_Arts_and_Sciences "College of Arts and Sciences"), [Science and Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science_and_Technology "Science and Technology"), Enugu, was incorporated into the university in 1961, and its buildings now form the Enugu Campus [(200 hectares](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hectare "Hectare")) of the university located in the heart of Enugu, the administrative capital of Enugu State of Nigeria. Enugu is a modern city, accessible by air, rail and road. [The Faculties of Business Administration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Business_administration "Business administration"), [Environmental Studies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Environmental_studies "Environmental studies"), [Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Law "Law"), Basic Medical Sciences, and [Health Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Health_Sciences "Health Sciences") are located at the Enugu Campus.

The teaching hospital attached to the university is presently sited at Ituku-Ozalla (25 kilometres south of Enugu) on a 500-hectare (1,200-acre) site. It also hosts the [Faculty of Dentistry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faculty_of_Dentistry "Faculty of Dentistry")/[Dental Surgery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dental_surgery "Dental surgery") and [Medical Sciences](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Medical_sciences "Medical sciences").

The Aba campus (UNAC) hosts the National Institute for Nigerian Languages.

A former campus was opened in October 1973 in [Calabar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Calabar "Calabar"), [Cross River State](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_River_State "Cross River State"). The campus at Calabar became a full-fledged [University of Calabar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Calabar "University of Calabar") in October 1975.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-13)

The official name of the university is the University of Nigeria[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-14) and the official acronym is UNN. "[UN"](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations "United Nations") stands for University of Nigeria while the last "N" stands for Nsukka. This acronym is also shared by the main campus of the university, Nsukka (University of Nigeria, Nsukka). Thus technically, the name University of Nigeria, Nsukka refers to the main campus at Nsukka only while the name University of Nigeria refers to all the campuses of the university. References may be made to the location of the other campuses by mentioning the names of the cities where they are situated rather than a blanket description with the name Nsukka. Students at the Enugu Campus prefer to write the name of their school as University of Nigeria Enugu Campus (UNEC)[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-15) if they must add the location of their school. Students from other campuses of the school also prefer same. Official documents of the school describes the school as simply University of Nigeria. They also make this dichotomy when referring to different campuses of the school.

## Academics

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Nigeria&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Academics")]

Novelist [Chinua Achebe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinua_Achebe "Chinua Achebe") held research and teaching appointments at the university, beginning in the early 1970s. He worked in the faculty of arts with critic and [African literature](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_literature "African literature") scholar [Donatus Nwoga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donatus_Nwoga "Donatus Nwoga").[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-34) Astrophysicist [Sam Okoye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Ejikeme_Okoye "Samuel Ejikeme Okoye") founded the Space Research Center in 1972. The Centre for Basic Space Research remains one of the few institutions in Africa that carries out research and offers courses in astronomy at both the undergraduate and postgraduate levels.

The first open heart surgical operation in Nigeria and [sub-Saharan Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sub-Saharan_Africa "Sub-Saharan Africa") was undertaken in 1974 at the University of Nigeria Teaching Hospital (UNTH) Enugu. The team was led by visiting [Magdi Yacoub](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magdi_Yacoub "Magdi Yacoub") from the UK and others in the team included Professors [Fabian Udekwu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fabian_Udekwu "Fabian Udekwu") and Anyanwu. The College of Medicine has since evolved into the centre for cardiothoracic surgery and tropical cardiology excellence for the West Africa region with the siting of the National Cardiothoracic Center at UNTH Enugu. Much medical research is also being carried out in the college.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-35)

The Department of Fine and Applied Arts is known for the [Nsukka group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nsukka_group "Nsukka group") – seven artists associated with a system of traditional [Igbo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Igbo_people "Igbo people") designs and styles known as _[uli](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uli\_(design) "Uli (design)")_.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-37)

The Law Faculty of the university is the oldest in Nigeria; it was established in 1960.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-38)

The Department of Electronic Engineering was named a Center of Excellence in Electronics by the Federal Government of Nigeria in 1982. The department was established in 1981 under the faculty of engineering after the previous department of electronic engineering was split into two separate department.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-39) The department offers a Bachelor of Engineering degree in Electronic Engineering to undergraduates, as well a MSC and Doctoral degree program in relevant specializations under Electronic Engineering. The Department has produced the highest number of first-class graduate than any other department in the university. The department has also produced many overall best graduating students more than any department in the university. It has produced overall university best for the three consecutive academic session in 1995/1996 1996/1997 1997/1998.

### Library

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Nigeria&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Library")]

The University of Nigeria, Nsukka Libraries consist of the Nnamdi Azikiwe Library, the Enugu Campus Main Library and the Medical Library located at the College of Medicine, University of Nigeria Teaching Hospital, Ituku-Ozalla. On 8 March 2009, the multi-complex [Nnamdi Azikiwe Library of University of Nigeria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nnamdi_Azikiwe_Library "Nnamdi Azikiwe Library"), Nsukka was officially opened by the then minister of Education, Dr [Sam Egwu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Egwu "Sam Egwu").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-Eke-2014-40) The library has embraced information technology to provide an effective library service to users and this was why it was one of the three leading academic libraries in Nigeria where [TINLIB](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tinlib "Tinlib") software was introduced in the 90s.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-41) After so many failed attempts to [automate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Automation "Automation") the library using a well robust integrated library management software, the library finally settled for [KOHA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koha_(software) "Koha (software)") Integrated library management software to automate its activities.[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-42) The library collection is unique because it contains an [Africana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africana_(artifacts) "Africana (artifacts)") section that houses rare books such as Biafrana and Achebeana. It has a total holding of 350,000 book titles and about 5000 serials titles.[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria,_Nsukka#cite_note-Eke-2014-40)

The **University of Nairobi** (**UoN**; [Swahili](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swahili_language "Swahili language"): _Chuo Kikuu cha Nairobi_)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nairobi#cite_note-3) is a [collegiate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College "College")[research university](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Research_university "Research university") based in [Nairobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi "Nairobi") and is the largest [university](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_universities_and_colleges_in_Kenya "List of universities and colleges in Kenya") in [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nairobi#cite_note-4) Although its history as an [educational institution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Educational_institution "Educational institution") dates back to 1956, it did not become an independent university until 1970. During that year, the [University of East Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_East_Africa "University of East Africa") was split into three independent universities: the [Makerere University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Makerere_University "Makerere University") in [Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda "Uganda"), the [University of Dar es Salaam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Dar_es_Salaam "University of Dar es Salaam") in [Tanzania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanzania "Tanzania"), and the University of Nairobi in Kenya.

During the 2023 academic year, the university had 49,047 students, of whom 35,897 were [undergraduates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Undergraduates "Undergraduates") and 11,003 were [postgraduates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Postgraduates "Postgraduates").[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nairobi#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nairobi#cite_note-6) The university launched several policy frameworks and introduced self-funded enrollment (also called 'module 2') to cope with the rising demand for [higher education in Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Higher_education_in_Kenya "Higher education in Kenya").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nairobi#cite_note-7)

## Establishment

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Nairobi&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Establishment")]

The inception of the University of Nairobi dates back to 1956, with the establishment of the Royal Technical College, which admitted its first group of [A-level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A-level "A-level") graduates for technical courses in April of the same year. The Royal Technical College was transformed into the second university college in [East Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Africa "East Africa") on 25 June 1961 by the Scottish mathematician Professor [James Morton Hyslop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_Morton_Hyslop "James Morton Hyslop"),[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nairobi#cite_note-8) formerly of the [University of Witwatersrand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Witwatersrand "University of Witwatersrand") under the name Royal College of Nairobi.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nairobi#cite_note-9) It joined the [University of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_London "University of London")'s ['schemes of special relations'](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_London#Colleges_in_special_relation "University of London") and began preparing students in the faculties of [Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arts "Arts"), [Science](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Science "Science") and [Engineering](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Engineering "Engineering") for University of London award degrees. Meanwhile, students in other faculties such as the Faculty of Special Professional Studies (later renamed Faculty of Commerce) and Faculty of [Architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Architecture "Architecture") continued to offer diplomas for qualifications of professional bodies/institutions.

On 20 May 1964, the Royal College of Nairobi was renamed University College Nairobi as a [constituent college](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constituent_college "Constituent college") of the Federal University of East Africa. During this time, enrolled students studied for college degrees awarded by the [University of East Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_East_Africa "University of East Africa") instead of the University of London. In 1970, it transformed into the first [national university](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_university "National university") in [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya") and was renamed the University of Nairobi. The university tops in Kenya's [university ranking](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_ranking "University ranking"). It is ranked 7th in [Africa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Africa "Africa") and 1698 in the world according to [Webometrics Ranking of World Universities](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Webometrics_Ranking_of_World_Universities "Webometrics Ranking of World Universities").[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Nairobi&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: History")]

[![Image 7](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4d/Old_offices_at_UoN_used_by_colonialists.jpg/250px-Old_offices_at_UoN_used_by_colonialists.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Old_offices_at_UoN_used_by_colonialists.jpg)
