Ram's Horns: "Dweninmen" (Akan word for ram's horn) is an Adinkra symbol.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Ghana#cite_note-:1-19) Here, two interlocking ram's horns (DWENINMENTOASO) have been used to symbolise strength and a call to pursue a path of integrity.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Ghana#cite_note-:1-19) The University of Ghana was granted degree-awarding status in 1961.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Ghana#cite_note-20)

## History

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Ghana&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: History")]

The formation of the West African Commission of the Asquith Commission on Higher Education in the Colonies[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Ghana#cite_note-unigh-8) under the chairmanship of Rt. Hon. Walter Elliot[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Ghana#cite_note-unigh-8) was the birth of this institution in 1948.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Ghana#cite_note-unigh-8) The commission recommended the setting up of university colleges in association with the [University of London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_London "University of London"), thus the University College of the Gold Coast was founded by Ordinance on 11 August 1948 for the purpose of providing for and promoting university education, learning and research.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Ghana#cite_note-unigh-8) The people of Gold Coast rejected the recommendation that a single university college be established for the entire British West Africa region, with the college located in Nigeria. This rejection made it possible for the University of Ghana to be established.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Ghana#cite_note-21)

In the book commissioned by the University of Ghana, [Professor Francis Agbodeka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francis_Agbodeka "Francis Agbodeka") (1998) found that "Two members of the Legislative Council on their own volition worked on the question of securing funds for the project. More significant, F. M. Bourret (1949), in almost a contemporaneous account, reported that the strong and united opinion expressed by Dr. Nanka-Bruce in a Radio Station Zoy address to the People of the Gold Coast in October 1947, "was largely instrumental in influencing the Secretary of State for the colonies" to finally give his consent in 1947, "for the establishment of a Gold Coast University College."[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Ghana#cite_note-22)

Significantly, the establishment of the University of Ghana, based on the Elliot Commission's Majority Report (of which Sir Arku Korsah of the Gold Coast was a member), was the culmination of immense work of several organizations, committees, institutions, and prominent individuals, at home and abroad. Among some of the most prominent [Ghanaians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghanaians "Ghanaians"), members of organizations and civil society groups that campaigned for the establishment of the University of College of the Gold Coast/Ghana, included also Dr. Nanka-Bruce, Rev. Prof. C. G. Baeta, and Sir E. Asafu-Adjaye, Dr. J. B. and Danquah.

In 1961 the [Government of Ghana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Government_of_Ghana "Government of Ghana") under [Kwame Nkrumah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kwame_Nkrumah "Kwame Nkrumah") passed the University of Ghana Act, 1961 (Act 79) to replace the University College of Ghana. Through that act, the university attained sovereign university status and mandate to award its own degrees.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Ghana#cite_note-23)

### International Programmes Office

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Ghana&action=edit&section=13 "Edit section: International Programmes Office")]

The University of Ghana's International Programmes Office (IPO) was established in 1997 to harmonize the university's international efforts. It promotes all international activities, including admission of [international students](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_student "International student"), Memorandums of Understanding between the University and International educational institutions, visiting scholars, study abroad programmes, staff and student exchange programmes and research collaboration. The university has over 200 agreements with educational institutions all over the world, and works with organizations such as the [Council on International Educational Exchange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_on_International_Educational_Exchange "Council on International Educational Exchange") (CIEE), [California State University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/California_State_University "California State University") (CSU), University of California Education Abroad Program (UCEAP), and International Society of Education Planners International Student Exchange Programs to facilitate student exchange programmes.

### Halls of residence

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Ghana&action=edit&section=24 "Edit section: Halls of residence")]

Halls of residence are provided for Graduate and Undergraduate Students. There are main halls of residence by the Government of Ghana and private halls of residence built on the campus by individuals and corporate bodies.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Ghana#cite_note-59)[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Ghana#cite_note-JCRs_{{!}}_UG_{{!}}_Students-60) Below are descriptions of the halls of residence; Commonwealth Hall, Legon Hall, Mensah Sarbah Hall, Volta Hall, [Akuafo Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akuafo_Hall "Akuafo Hall") and Jubilee Hall at the University of Ghana, Legon.

*   **Commonwealth Hall** (the university's only male hall of residence). Known as the Vandals, the word VANDALS is an acronym for Vivacious, Affable, Neighborly, Devoted, Altruistic and Loyal. The students of Commonwealth Hall recognize themselves by calling out the word 'V-Mate' with a response word 'Sharp'. Often clad in red, as the colour of their identity, VANDALs pride themselves with unity.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Ghana#cite_note-61)
*   **Legon Hall** (The Legon Hall is the premier hall of the University of Ghana). Legon Hall was the first hall of residence to be built on the University of Ghana campus, thus referred to as the Premier Hall. The Hall is located at the Centre of the school close to the Balme Library. Just like the Mensah Sarbah Hall and the Akuafo Hall, Legon Hall serves as home for both male and female students, allowing for strong bonds between the sexes on the campus.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Ghana#cite_note-62) The motto of the Legon hall is; "_Cui Multidum Datum"_, which means "_human relations with examples_".[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Ghana#cite_note-63)
*   **Mensah Sarbah Hall** (The Mensah Sarbah Hall is the first hall to be named after a hero of the nation; [John Mensah Sarbah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Mensah_Sarbah "John Mensah Sarbah")). The hall is recognised to host most of the best athletes on the university's campus.
*   **Volta Hall** (the university's female-only hall of residence). It is the only all-female hall on the campus known for their discipline and neatness. The hall has churned out many respectable women such as the first female Chief [Justice Georgina Theodora Woode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Georgina_Theodora_Wood "Georgina Theodora Wood").
*   **[Akuafo Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akuafo_Hall "Akuafo Hall")** The word "_akuafo_" is an Akan word which means farmers. For this reason the hall is notably called the Farmers hall with a rich Ghanaian culture and tradition. The Akuafo Hall was the second hall of residence to be established in the University of Ghana. Their chieftaincy institution serves as a symbol of unity for students and also helps to promote and showcase the rich Ghanaian culture. The chief farmer and his queen mother are elected annually.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Ghana#cite_note-64)
*   **Jubilee Hall.** The Jubilee Hall is one of the halls of residence of the University of Ghana, Legon. The Jubilee hall is located on the south of the university campus, and opposite to the International Students Hostel. Jubilee Hall was built to commemorate the university's Golden Jubilee celebration in 1998. The hall was mainly built through support funds from alumni of the university.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Ghana#cite_note-65)

The university has eight newly created halls of residence that were commissioned in 2011. They are:

*   **Alexander Kwapong Hall**, named after Professor [Alexander Kwapong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Kwapong "Alexander Kwapong") a former Vice-Chancellor and Chairman of the Council of State.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Ghana#cite_note-66)
*   **Jean Nelson Akah Hall**, named after an alumnus, Jean Nelson Akah. It was inaugurated in July 2010. Its emblem shows a candle, a book and a pen to symbolize perseverance. It was designed by a final year Physics-Computer Science major student Raymond Sung-Seh Harrison. The motto of the hall, "_Lux in Tenebris_", which is Latin for "_Light in Darkness_", was suggested by Raymond's mate at the time, a lady by the name Muna Twerefour. The emblem was officially adopted on Tuesday, 2 April 2013.
*   **Hilla Limann Hall**, the first of the University of Ghana Enterprise Limited (UGEL) hostels to be completed. It was inaugurated in July 2010,[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Ghana#cite_note-67) during which the Vice-Chancellor announced the decision to name it after [Dr. Hilla Limann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilla_Limann "Hilla Limann"), a former President of the Republic of Ghana. Senior members of the university may be assigned as Fellows of the Hall by the Vice Chancellor. Students assigned/affiliated to the Hall form the Junior members. The Head of the Hall, Senior Tutor and fellow tutors serve as a body which helps with the governing of the Hall.
*   **Elizabeth Sey Hall**, the second of the newer halls built by University of Ghana Enterprise Limited (UGEL) Hostels to be completed. It was inaugurated in July 2010 and was named after the first female graduate of the university, [Elizabeth Frances Baaba Sey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_Frances_Sey "Elizabeth Frances Sey").
*   **Africa Union Hall**, formerly called Pentagon, built by [Social Security and National Insurance Trust (SSNIT)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/SSNIT "SSNIT").
*   **James Topp Nelson Yankah Hall**, formerly known as Teachers Fund (TF) Hostel.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Ghana#cite_note-68)
*   **Bani Hall**, initially a private hostel and later had transferred to the status of a hall after the tenancy agreement with the university had elapsed.
*   **Evandy Hall**, formerly Evandy Hostel and this was turned into a hall after the tenancy agreement with the university elapsed and ownership transferred to University authority.

### Roads usage and user charges

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Ghana&action=edit&section=27 "Edit section: Roads usage and user charges")]

From 1 February 2014, all vehicles entering the University of Ghana's main campus, and also those using the road passing through the Staff Village of the university were required to pay charges. This was heavily criticized by public and students and was therefore suspended.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Ghana#cite_note-70) Currently, various entry points into the campus require vehicle owners (typically staff and students) to obtain electronically scannable cards issued and authorized by the transport unit of the university.

## Controversy

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Ghana&action=edit&section=30 "Edit section: Controversy")]

The management of the university was labeled as 'insensitive' to the hardship caused by the [COVID-19 pandemic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19_pandemic "COVID-19 pandemic") after the school increased its facility user fees for 2020/21 academic year. It led to a protest on social media and the decision was later reversed.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Ghana#cite_note-80) In recent years there has been reports of sexual misconduct levelled against several lecturers at the university which the university denied. An investigative documentary was produced by former victims of the sexual harassment which was uploaded to YouTube.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Ghana#cite_note-81)[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Ghana#cite_note-82)[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Ghana#cite_note-83)

## UG Sports Stadium

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=University_of_Ghana&action=edit&section=31 "Edit section: UG Sports Stadium")]

The University of Ghana Sports Stadium is located in Accra. The venue, which has a capacity of 10,000,[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Ghana#cite_note-84) opened in 2024 by the Vice President of Ghana on March 21.[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Ghana#cite_note-85) The stadium is used mostly for [association football](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Association_football "Association football") and [rugby union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rugby_union "Rugby union"). It also has an athletics track. The facility was built as a legacy of the school. It also marks the 75th Anniversary of the University.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Ghana#cite_note-86)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

South African painter (born 1948)

**Gavin Jantjes** (born 1948 in [District Six](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/District_Six "District Six"), [Cape Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Town "Cape Town")) is a South African painter, curator, writer and lecturer.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gavin_Jantjes#cite_note-Donnell2002-1)

## Life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gavin_Jantjes&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Life")]

Jantjes attended the [Michaelis School of Fine Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michaelis_School_of_Fine_Art "Michaelis School of Fine Art") at the [University of Cape Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Cape_Town "University of Cape Town") from 1966 to 1969. He left apartheid South Africa in 1970 on a DAAD scholarship to study at the [Hochschule für bildende Künste Hamburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hochschule_f%C3%BCr_bildende_K%C3%BCnste_Hamburg "Hochschule für bildende Künste Hamburg") between 1970 and 1972. He was a founding member of the [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany") anti-[apartheid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apartheid "Apartheid") movement. He was granted political asylum in Germany in 1973. He worked as a consultant visual campaign director for the [United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_High_Commissioner_for_Refugees "United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees") from 1978 to 1982. In 1979 he published the _South African Colouring Book_, which consisted of eleven collaged serigraphs exploring apartheid in the format of a child's coloring book.

He moved his studio to Wiltshire, England in 1982. In 1986 he was appointed a Senior Lecturer in Fine Art at [Chelsea College of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chelsea_College_of_Arts "Chelsea College of Arts"), The London Institute. From 1986 to 1990 he was on the council of the [Arts Council of Great Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arts_Council_of_Great_Britain "Arts Council of Great Britain") and was its consultant for the formation of the Institute of New International Visual Art ([InIVA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/InIVA "InIVA")). He also served on the advisory board of the [Tate Liverpool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tate_Liverpool "Tate Liverpool") from 1992 until 1995, and was a trustee of London's [Serpentine Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serpentine_Gallery "Serpentine Gallery") from 1995 until 1998.

He became artistic director of the [Henie Onstad Kunstsenter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henie_Onstad_Kunstsenter "Henie Onstad Kunstsenter"), Hovikodden, near Oslo in 1998 and curated one person exhibitions there of [Gordon Bennett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gordon_Bennett_(artist) "Gordon Bennett (artist)"), [Yinka Shonibare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yinka_Shonibare "Yinka Shonibare"), [Susan Hiller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susan_Hiller "Susan Hiller"), [Marie-Jo Lafontaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie-Jo_Lafontaine "Marie-Jo Lafontaine"), [Shirin Neshat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shirin_Neshat "Shirin Neshat"), [Marlene Dumas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marlene_Dumas "Marlene Dumas") and [Carlos Capelan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Capelan "Carlos Capelan").

In 2004 he joined the [National Museum of Art, Architecture and Design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_Art,_Architecture_and_Design "National Museum of Art, Architecture and Design"), Oslo, as its Senior Consultant for International Contemporary Exhibitions: he curated exhibitions there on [Amar Kanwar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amar_Kanwar "Amar Kanwar"), [Harun Farocki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harun_Farocki "Harun Farocki") and [Nicholas Hlobo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_Hlobo "Nicholas Hlobo"). He was also the Project Director of the Visual Century Project on 20th Century and contemporary South African resulting in the publication, Visual Century: South African Art in Context (2011).

He left the National Museum in 2014 and reopened his studio in Oslo in 2015. He continues to paint, moving between Cape Town, England and Oslo.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

South African painter (born 1948)

**Gavin Jantjes** (born 1948 in [District Six](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/District_Six "District Six"), [Cape Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Town "Cape Town")) is a South African painter, curator, writer and lecturer.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gavin_Jantjes#cite_note-Donnell2002-1)

## Life

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gavin_Jantjes&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Life")]

Jantjes attended the [Michaelis School of Fine Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Michaelis_School_of_Fine_Art "Michaelis School of Fine Art") at the [University of Cape Town](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Cape_Town "University of Cape Town") from 1966 to 1969. He left apartheid South Africa in 1970 on a DAAD scholarship to study at the [Hochschule für bildende Künste Hamburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hochschule_f%C3%BCr_bildende_K%C3%BCnste_Hamburg "Hochschule für bildende Künste Hamburg") between 1970 and 1972. He was a founding member of the [German](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany") anti-[apartheid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apartheid "Apartheid") movement. He was granted political asylum in Germany in 1973. He worked as a consultant visual campaign director for the [United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Nations_High_Commissioner_for_Refugees "United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees") from 1978 to 1982. In 1979 he published the _South African Colouring Book_, which consisted of eleven collaged serigraphs exploring apartheid in the format of a child's coloring book.

He moved his studio to Wiltshire, England in 1982. In 1986 he was appointed a Senior Lecturer in Fine Art at [Chelsea College of Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chelsea_College_of_Arts "Chelsea College of Arts"), The London Institute. From 1986 to 1990 he was on the council of the [Arts Council of Great Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arts_Council_of_Great_Britain "Arts Council of Great Britain") and was its consultant for the formation of the Institute of New International Visual Art ([InIVA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/InIVA "InIVA")). He also served on the advisory board of the [Tate Liverpool](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tate_Liverpool "Tate Liverpool") from 1992 until 1995, and was a trustee of London's [Serpentine Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Serpentine_Gallery "Serpentine Gallery") from 1995 until 1998.

He became artistic director of the [Henie Onstad Kunstsenter](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henie_Onstad_Kunstsenter "Henie Onstad Kunstsenter"), Hovikodden, near Oslo in 1998 and curated one person exhibitions there of [Gordon Bennett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gordon_Bennett_(artist) "Gordon Bennett (artist)"), [Yinka Shonibare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yinka_Shonibare "Yinka Shonibare"), [Susan Hiller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susan_Hiller "Susan Hiller"), [Marie-Jo Lafontaine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marie-Jo_Lafontaine "Marie-Jo Lafontaine"), [Shirin Neshat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shirin_Neshat "Shirin Neshat"), [Marlene Dumas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marlene_Dumas "Marlene Dumas") and [Carlos Capelan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Capelan "Carlos Capelan").

In 2004 he joined the [National Museum of Art, Architecture and Design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_Art,_Architecture_and_Design "National Museum of Art, Architecture and Design"), Oslo, as its Senior Consultant for International Contemporary Exhibitions: he curated exhibitions there on [Amar Kanwar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amar_Kanwar "Amar Kanwar"), [Harun Farocki](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harun_Farocki "Harun Farocki") and [Nicholas Hlobo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicholas_Hlobo "Nicholas Hlobo"). He was also the Project Director of the Visual Century Project on 20th Century and contemporary South African resulting in the publication, Visual Century: South African Art in Context (2011).

He left the National Museum in 2014 and reopened his studio in Oslo in 2015. He continues to paint, moving between Cape Town, England and Oslo.

## Exhibitions

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gavin_Jantjes&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Exhibitions")]

One man shows of work by Gavin Jantjes include:

*   1970 The Artists Gallery, Cape Town
*   1976 Institute of Contemporary Arts (ICA), London and Henie Onstad Art Centre, Hovikodden
*   1977 Provinciehuis, Groningen
*   1978 Kulturhuset, Stockholm
*   1979 Kunsterhaus Bethanien, Berlin
*   1980–3, 1986, 1990 Edward Totah Gallery, London
*   1984 Midland Group, Nottingham
*   1985 Black Art Gallery, London
*   1987 Blue Coat Gallery, Liverpool
*   1988 Herbert Museum and Art Gallery, Coventry
*   1989 City Museums and Art Gallery, Stoke-on-Trent
*   2024 Whitechapel Gallery, London

## Collections

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Gavin_Jantjes&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Collections")]

Jantjes’ work in is the collections of [Tate Britain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tate_Britain "Tate Britain"), London; [Victoria and Albert Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Victoria_and_Albert_Museum "Victoria and Albert Museum"), London; [Arts Council Collection](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arts_Council_Collection "Arts Council Collection"); [Wolverhampton Art Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolverhampton_Art_Gallery "Wolverhampton Art Gallery"); Coventry City Museum; [National Museum of African Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_African_Art "National Museum of African Art"), Smithsonian Institution, Washington, D.C.

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Ghanaian artist (born 1944)

| El Anatsui |
| --- |
| Born | (1944-02-04) 4 February 1944 (age 82) [Anyako, Volta Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anyako,_Volta_Region "Anyako, Volta Region"), Ghana |
| Known for | [Visual Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_Art "Visual Art"), [Sculpture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sculpture "Sculpture") |
| Awards | [Prince Claus Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Claus_Fund "Prince Claus Fund") |

**El Anatsui** ([/ɛ l ˌ æ n ə t ˈ s uː i/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); born 4 February 1944)[[1]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-1)[[2]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-2)[[3]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-3) is a Ghanaian [sculptor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sculptor "Sculptor") active for much of his career in Nigeria. He has drawn particular international attention for his "[bottle-top](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bottle_cap "Bottle cap") installations". These installations consist of thousands of [aluminum pieces sourced](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium_recycling "Aluminium recycling") from alcohol recycling stations and sewn together with copper wire, which are then transformed into metallic cloth-like wall sculptures. Such materials, while seemingly stiff and sturdy, are actually free and flexible, which often helps with manipulation when installing his sculptures.[[4]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-4)[[5]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-5)

Anatsui was included in the 2023 [_Time_ 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_100 "Time 100") list of the world's most influential people.[[6]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:6-6) In the article, artist and art historian Okeke-Agulu writes, "The breathtaking combination of experimental rigor and inspired vision turns such unassuming materials as printer's plates or liquor-bottle caps into the magnificent constructions and compositions displayed around the world."[[6]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:6-6)

## Early life and education

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

El Anatsui was born in [Anyako](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anyako "Anyako"), in the [Volta Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volta_Region "Volta Region") of Ghana. The youngest of his father's 32 children, Anatsui lost his mother and was raised by his uncle. His first experience with art was through drawing letters on a chalkboard.[[7]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:3-7) His lettering attempts drew the attention of his school's headmaster, who encouraged his effort by providing him with more chalk. Because of his age at the time (just after kindergarten), he regarded the letters more as images than as letters--the forms interested him.[[8]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:4-8)

Anatsui received his B.A in 1968 from the [College of Art and Built Environment (KNUST)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_of_Art_and_Built_Environment_(KNUST) "College of Art and Built Environment (KNUST)") in Kumasi, Ghana. He received his postgraduate diploma in Art Education the following year, in 1969, from [Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kwame_Nkrumah_University_of_Science_and_Technology "Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology"), also in Kumasi.[[9]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:5-9)

Some of his early artistic influences include [Oku Ampofo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oku_Ampofo "Oku Ampofo"), [Vincent Akwete Kofi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_Kofi "Vincent Kofi"), and [Kofi Antubam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kofi_Antubam "Kofi Antubam"), all of whom began to reject foreign influences in their practices in favor of indigenous art forms.[[10]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-10) After graduating in 1969, Anatsui assumed a teaching position at Winneba Specialist Training College (now [University of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Education,_Winneba "University of Education, Winneba")), a role that had previously been filled by Kofi.[[7]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:3-7)

He began teaching at the [University of Nigeria, Nsukka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria "University of Nigeria") in 1975.[[11]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-NMOAA-11) He became a senior lecturer for the Fine and Applied Arts department in 1982, and later became head of that department and full professor of sculpture in 1996, a role he occupied until 2011.[[9]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:5-9) His presence at the University of Nsukka led to his affiliation with the [Nsukka group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nsukka_group "Nsukka group").

> It has taken many years to find artists who can occupy a prominent place on the global circuit while choosing to reside outside the [metropolitan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_area "Metropolitan area") centres. [William Kentridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Kentridge "William Kentridge") has made his reputation from [Johannesburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannesburg "Johannesburg"), and El Anatsui has conquered the planet while living and working in the Nigerian university town of Nsukka.[[12]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-12)

## Artwork

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Artwork")]

Anatsui notes that, through school and in university, "everything we were doing was western," especially within the fine arts department of his university; he felt that there was something missing in his education for its lack of focus on his own culture.[[13]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:2-13) In order to rectify this, he started visiting the National Cultural Centre of Ghana, also in Kumasi, to engage with the musicians, graphic artists, textile artists, printers, and creative artists of all types. It was there that he encountered [Adinkra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adinkra_symbols "Adinkra symbols"), a system of signs and symbols, which was his first introduction to abstract art and opened up a new world of artistic possibilities for him.[[13]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:2-13)

In the 1970s, Anatsui worked frequently in wood. He was particularly interested in wooden trays, which he often saw used in the markets to display food items and other wares--he would carve them or engrave them with Adinkra symbols and other marks using hot rods.[[8]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:4-8) He also began using wood to construct wall panels from strips placed next to each other, the surface decorated with designs imparted on the material through the use of chain saws, gouges, flame, or paint.[[11]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-NMOAA-11) In the late 70s, he began working in clay: pots, in particular, exploring themes of fragility and dilapidation. He was interested in how, even after a pot breaks and ceases being used in the way we commonly think (for food, water), it takes on a new purpose, even acquires more uses, from the mundane to the spiritual. Most intriguing to him is the use of pot shards for presenting offerings. He said, "It's as if the pot, having broken, is transformed into a dimension which makes it ideal for use by ancestors and deities who are themselves in the spirit dimension."[[8]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:4-8)

After his work with the broken pots, Anatsui explored food-adjacent themes in other materials: wood, again, in the form of mortars; equipment used to process [cassava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassava "Cassava"), and bottle tops.[[8]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:4-8)

Much of Anatsui's work features found materials, or materials that had a life of use prior to being formed into this artworks. His emphasis on the found object, however, is less [Duchampian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcel_Duchamp "Marcel Duchamp"), and more focused on the history of use and the evidence of the human hand in the material.[[8]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:4-8)

> "When something has been used, there is a certain charge, a certain energy, that has to do with the people who have touched it and used it and sometimes abused it. This helps to direct what one is doing, and also to root what one is doing in the environment and the culture."[[13]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:2-13)

Metal bottle caps are a favorite material of his; like cloth, Anatsui describes, an arrangement of bottle caps is versatile, allowing him to consider his art both sculpturally (through the form of the caps) and in a painterly manner (through the colors of the caps). Further, he appreciates the glimpse that bottle caps give into current and historical political and sociological issues, by virtue of the names and colors of various drink brands that are printed onto the caps.[[13]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:2-13)

> "The most important thing for me is the transformation. The fact that these media, each identifying a brand of drink, are no longer going back to serve the same role but are elements that could generate some reflection, some thinking, or just some wonder. This is possible because they are removed from their accustomed, functional context into a new one, and they bring along their histories and identities."[[8]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:4-8)

A number of themes are present in Anatsui's work: the destruction and subsequent reconstitution of material as a metaphor for life and the changes Africa faced under colonialism and since independence; traditional themes and motifs of West African strip woven cloth and other [African textiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_textiles "African textiles"); and concern over Western scholarly misinterpretation of African history and the distortions it has caused.[[11]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-NMOAA-11) His work is also thematically connected to the West African cultural landscape and ideas of consumption and labor.[[8]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:4-8)

The idea of [Sankofa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sankofa "Sankofa") [translated as "go back and retrieve"] is also present in Anatsui's work. He views it as a way of drawing on the past, the lessons it offers, to chart a mode of moving forward. For him, Sankofa described a need to draw from what was immediately around him; Ghana became independent when he was in high school, and much of his education had been focused on western art and art history, and so he felt called to 'go back and retrieve' aspects of Ghanaian culture that had been suppressed, something he described as a sort of "quest for self-discovery."[[8]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:4-8)

## Exhibitions

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Exhibitions")]

[![Image 4](http://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8f/El_Anatsui_-_Man%27s_Cloth.jpg/250px-El_Anatsui_-_Man%27s_Cloth.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:El_Anatsui_-_Man's_Cloth.jpg)

_Man's Cloth_ (1998–2001) at the [British Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Museum "British Museum") in 2009

Anatsui's career grew gradually, starting in his home village of [Nsukka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nsukka "Nsukka") before branching off to places such as [Enugu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enugu_(city) "Enugu (city)") and [Lagos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagos "Lagos"), and eventually internationally.[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14) In 1990, Anatsui had his first important group show at the [Studio Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studio_Museum_in_Harlem "Studio Museum in Harlem") In [Harlem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harlem "Harlem"), [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)"). He also was one of three artists singled out in the 1990 exhibition "Contemporary African Artists: Changing Traditions", which was extended for five years.[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14) Anatsui has since exhibited his work around the world, including at the [Brooklyn Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Museum "Brooklyn Museum") (2013);[[15]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-15) the [Clark Art Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clark_Art_Institute "Clark Art Institute") (2011);[[16]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-16) the Rice University Art Gallery, Houston (2010);[[17]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-17) the [Metropolitan Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Museum_of_Art "Metropolitan Museum of Art"), New York (2008–09);[[18]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-18) the [National Museum of African Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_African_Art "National Museum of African Art"), Smithsonian Institution, Washington, D.C. (2008);[[19]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-19) the [Fowler Museum at UCLA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fowler_Museum_at_UCLA "Fowler Museum at UCLA") (2007);[[20]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-20) the [Venice Biennale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice_Biennale "Venice Biennale") (1990 and 2007);[[21]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-interview-21) the [Hayward Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hayward_Gallery "Hayward Gallery") (2005);[[22]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-22) the [Liverpool Biennial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool_Biennial "Liverpool Biennial") (2002);[[21]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-interview-21) the National Museum of African Art (2001);[[21]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-interview-21) the [Centre de Cultura Contemporània de Barcelona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centre_de_Cultura_Contempor%C3%A0nia_de_Barcelona "Centre de Cultura Contemporània de Barcelona") (2001);[[21]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-interview-21) the 8th Osaka Sculpture Triennale (1995);[[21]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-interview-21) the 5th [Gwangju Biennale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gwangju_Biennale "Gwangju Biennale") (2004); the [Arab Museum of Modern Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_Museum_of_Modern_Art "Arab Museum of Modern Art") in Doha (2019);[[23]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-Lucas_40-23) and the [Kunstmuseum Bern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kunstmuseum_Bern "Kunstmuseum Bern") (2020).[[24]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-24) In 1995, Anatsui held his first solo exhibition outside of Africa in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"). He expressed a variety of themes and demonstrated how African art can be shown in a multitude of ways that are not seen as "typical" African.[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14) His work utilized conceptual modes used by European and American artists but hardly in African countries.[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14) Anatsui showed his work at the de Young Museum in [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco") in 2005. This was his first time "appear[ing] as part of the permanent collection in a major art museum".[[25]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:0-25) Also in 2005, his exhibition at New York's [Skoto Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skoto_Gallery?action=edit&redlink=1 "Skoto Gallery (page does not exist)"), _Danudo_, was the first display of his metal sheets in an American city.[[25]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:0-25) At this gallery, Skoto Aghahowa presented Anatsui's wood wall panels alongside [Sol LeWitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sol_LeWitt "Sol LeWitt")'s drawings. This exhibition popularized his bottle-cap works as he gained more recognition in the press.[[25]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:0-25)

[![Image 5](http://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/68/Artempo_ElAnatsui.jpg/250px-Artempo_ElAnatsui.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Artempo_ElAnatsui.jpg)

Anatsui's [Palazzo Fortuny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Fortuny "Palazzo Fortuny") Artempo exhibition in 2007

Anatsui was invited to the [Venice Biennale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice_Biennale "Venice Biennale") in 2006 and again in 2007 where he was commissioned to make two hanging metal tapestries. During the 2007 edition, he exhibited his works at the [Palazzo Fortuny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Fortuny "Palazzo Fortuny") which consisted of newly built walls for him to display three metal hangings entitled _Dusasa_.[[25]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:0-25) Each artwork demonstrated different textures and colors including golds, reds, and blacks. The way the bottle tops draped throughout the hangings created a sense of gentleness that made it stand apart from the other works in the gallery.[[25]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:0-25) The art curator of the Biennale, [Robert Storr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Storr_(art_academic) "Robert Storr (art academic)"), mentions that the artist's series "reaches back into a whole series of things in the postwar period-it has a kind of exaltation I have not seen before".[[25]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:0-25) During this Venetian showing, Anatsui wanted to create a new experience for his viewers conceptually. He believes that "human life is not something which is cut and dried. It is something that is constantly in a state of change."[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14) At this point, he began to refer his metalworks as hangings instead of "cloths".[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14)

[![Image 6](http://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/f/f5/Another_Man%27s_Cloth%2C_2006%2C_El_Anatsui_at_Rubell_DC_2022.jpg/250px-Another_Man%27s_Cloth%2C_2006%2C_El_Anatsui_at_Rubell_DC_2022.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Another_Man's_Cloth,_2006,_El_Anatsui_at_Rubell_DC_2022.jpg)

_Another Man's Cloth_ (2006) at the [Rubell Museum DC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubell_Museum#Rubell_Museum_DC "Rubell Museum") in 2022

A 2010 retrospective of his work, entitled _When I Last Wrote to You About Africa_, was organized by the [Museum for African Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_for_African_Art "Museum for African Art") and opened at the [Royal Ontario Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Ontario_Museum "Royal Ontario Museum") in [Toronto, Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto "Toronto"), Canada. It subsequently toured venues in the United States for three years, concluding at the [University of Michigan Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Michigan_Museum_of_Art "University of Michigan Museum of Art").

A major exhibition of recent works, entitled _Gravity & Grace: Monumental Works by El Anatsui_, had its [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") premiere at the [Brooklyn Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Museum "Brooklyn Museum") in 2013. Organized by the [Akron Art Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akron_Art_Museum "Akron Art Museum") (exhibition: 2012), the exhibition later traveled to the [Des Moines Art Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Des_Moines_Art_Center "Des Moines Art Center") (2013–14) and the [Bass Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bass_Museum "Bass Museum") in Miami (2014).[[26]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-26)

A career-spanning survey of his work, organized by [Okwui Enwezor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okwui_Enwezor "Okwui Enwezor") and [Chika Okeke-Agulu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chika_Okeke-Agulu "Chika Okeke-Agulu"), entitled _Triumphant Scale_ drew record-breaking crowds when it opened in March 2019, at Munich's [Haus der Kunst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haus_der_Kunst "Haus der Kunst"). From there, the show travelled to the [Arab Museum of Modern Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_Museum_of_Modern_Art "Arab Museum of Modern Art"), in Doha, and later to the [Kunstmuseum Bern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kunstmuseum_Bern "Kunstmuseum Bern") in 2020.[[23]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-Lucas_40-23)

Anatsui was selected for the 2023 Hyundai Commission at the Turbine Hall at [Tate Modern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tate_Modern "Tate Modern"); a vast display space for large-scale sculptural and site-specific artworks. His work, _Behind the Red Moon_, is made of thousands of metal bottle tops and fragments, building upon his work with materials linked to the transatlantic slave trade, and was on view through 14 April 2024.[[27]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-27)[[28]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-28)[[29]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-29)

## Other activities

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Other activities")]

Anatsui was selected to be a member of the International Society for Education through Art (InSEA) world council in 1992 for his work in education.[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14) Anatsui was a founding member and fellow of the [Forum for African Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forum_for_African_Arts?action=edit&redlink=1 "Forum for African Arts (page does not exist)") in 2000. That year he also became a member of the International Selection Committee for the [Dakar Biennale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dakar_Biennale "Dakar Biennale") in Senegal.[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14) In 2001 he was a fellow at the [Civitella Ranieri Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civitella_Ranieri_Foundation "Civitella Ranieri Foundation") in Italy.[[30]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:1-30)[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14)

## Recognition

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Recognition")]

### Awards

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Awards")]

Anatsui won an honorable mention at the First [Ghana National Art Competition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghana_National_Art_Competition?action=edit&redlink=1 "Ghana National Art Competition (page does not exist)") as an undergraduate student in 1968. The following year he was awarded the Best Student of the Year at the [College of Art in Kumasi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_of_Art_in_Kumasi?action=edit&redlink=1 "College of Art in Kumasi (page does not exist)"), Ghana.[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14) In 1983 he won a commission for two large public sculptures made of terrazzo-surfaced cement on the [Nsukka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nsukka "Nsukka") campus.[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14) He was selected to be one of ten artists invited to the [Zweites Symposium Nordesekkuste](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zweites_Symposium_Nordesekkuste?action=edit&redlink=1 "Zweites Symposium Nordesekkuste (page does not exist)") residency in [Cuxhaven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuxhaven "Cuxhaven"), [West Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Germany "West Germany"), in 1984.[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14)

In 1990, Anatsui was invited to the 44th annual [Venice Biennale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice_Biennale "Venice Biennale") show _5 Contemporary African Artists_, where he received an honorable mention.[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14) That year he was included in the American documentary _Nigerian Art-Kindred Spirits_.

In 2015, the Venice Biennale awarded Anatsui the [Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice_Biennale#Awards "Venice Biennale").[[31]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-31)[[32]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-32) In 2017, Anatsui was awarded the [Praemium Imperiale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Praemium_Imperiale "Praemium Imperiale"), the first Ghanaian to win this international art prize.[[33]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-33)[[34]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-34)

Other awards include:

*   1990 – Public Prize, 7th Annual Triennale der Kleinplastik[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14)
*   1995 – Kansai Telecasting Prize, 6th Osaka Sculpture Triennial[[30]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:1-30)[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14)
*   1998 – Bronze Prize, 9th Osaka Sculpture Triennial[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14)
*   2008 – Visionaries! Award, [Museum of Arts and Design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Arts_and_Design "Museum of Arts and Design") (MAD)[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14)
*   2009 – [Prince Claus Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Claus_Fund "Prince Claus Fund")
*   2009 – Artist Honoree, 30th Anniversary Celebration, [National Museum of African Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_African_Art "National Museum of African Art")[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14)
*   2016 – Honorary doctorate, [Harvard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University")[[35]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-35)[[36]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-36)[[37]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-37)
*   2017 – Honorary doctorate, [Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kwame_Nkrumah_University_of_Science_and_Technology "Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology")[[38]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-38)[[39]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-39)
*   2023 – _[Time 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time\_100 "Time 100")_[[40]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-40)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Ghanaian artist (born 1944)

| El Anatsui |
| --- |
| Born | (1944-02-04) 4 February 1944 (age 82) [Anyako, Volta Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anyako,_Volta_Region "Anyako, Volta Region"), Ghana |
| Known for | [Visual Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Visual_Art "Visual Art"), [Sculpture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sculpture "Sculpture") |
| Awards | [Prince Claus Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Claus_Fund "Prince Claus Fund") |

**El Anatsui** ([/ɛ l ˌ æ n ə t ˈ s uː i/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English"); born 4 February 1944)[[1]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-1)[[2]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-2)[[3]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-3) is a Ghanaian [sculptor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sculptor "Sculptor") active for much of his career in Nigeria. He has drawn particular international attention for his "[bottle-top](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bottle_cap "Bottle cap") installations". These installations consist of thousands of [aluminum pieces sourced](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aluminium_recycling "Aluminium recycling") from alcohol recycling stations and sewn together with copper wire, which are then transformed into metallic cloth-like wall sculptures. Such materials, while seemingly stiff and sturdy, are actually free and flexible, which often helps with manipulation when installing his sculptures.[[4]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-4)[[5]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-5)

Anatsui was included in the 2023 [_Time_ 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time_100 "Time 100") list of the world's most influential people.[[6]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:6-6) In the article, artist and art historian Okeke-Agulu writes, "The breathtaking combination of experimental rigor and inspired vision turns such unassuming materials as printer's plates or liquor-bottle caps into the magnificent constructions and compositions displayed around the world."[[6]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:6-6)

## Early life and education

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

El Anatsui was born in [Anyako](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anyako "Anyako"), in the [Volta Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volta_Region "Volta Region") of Ghana. The youngest of his father's 32 children, Anatsui lost his mother and was raised by his uncle. His first experience with art was through drawing letters on a chalkboard.[[7]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:3-7) His lettering attempts drew the attention of his school's headmaster, who encouraged his effort by providing him with more chalk. Because of his age at the time (just after kindergarten), he regarded the letters more as images than as letters--the forms interested him.[[8]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:4-8)

Anatsui received his B.A in 1968 from the [College of Art and Built Environment (KNUST)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_of_Art_and_Built_Environment_(KNUST) "College of Art and Built Environment (KNUST)") in Kumasi, Ghana. He received his postgraduate diploma in Art Education the following year, in 1969, from [Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kwame_Nkrumah_University_of_Science_and_Technology "Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology"), also in Kumasi.[[9]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:5-9)

Some of his early artistic influences include [Oku Ampofo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oku_Ampofo "Oku Ampofo"), [Vincent Akwete Kofi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vincent_Kofi "Vincent Kofi"), and [Kofi Antubam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kofi_Antubam "Kofi Antubam"), all of whom began to reject foreign influences in their practices in favor of indigenous art forms.[[10]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-10) After graduating in 1969, Anatsui assumed a teaching position at Winneba Specialist Training College (now [University of Education](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Education,_Winneba "University of Education, Winneba")), a role that had previously been filled by Kofi.[[7]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:3-7)

He began teaching at the [University of Nigeria, Nsukka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Nigeria "University of Nigeria") in 1975.[[11]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-NMOAA-11) He became a senior lecturer for the Fine and Applied Arts department in 1982, and later became head of that department and full professor of sculpture in 1996, a role he occupied until 2011.[[9]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:5-9) His presence at the University of Nsukka led to his affiliation with the [Nsukka group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nsukka_group "Nsukka group").

> It has taken many years to find artists who can occupy a prominent place on the global circuit while choosing to reside outside the [metropolitan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_area "Metropolitan area") centres. [William Kentridge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Kentridge "William Kentridge") has made his reputation from [Johannesburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannesburg "Johannesburg"), and El Anatsui has conquered the planet while living and working in the Nigerian university town of Nsukka.[[12]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-12)

## Artwork

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Artwork")]

Anatsui notes that, through school and in university, "everything we were doing was western," especially within the fine arts department of his university; he felt that there was something missing in his education for its lack of focus on his own culture.[[13]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:2-13) In order to rectify this, he started visiting the National Cultural Centre of Ghana, also in Kumasi, to engage with the musicians, graphic artists, textile artists, printers, and creative artists of all types. It was there that he encountered [Adinkra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Adinkra_symbols "Adinkra symbols"), a system of signs and symbols, which was his first introduction to abstract art and opened up a new world of artistic possibilities for him.[[13]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:2-13)

In the 1970s, Anatsui worked frequently in wood. He was particularly interested in wooden trays, which he often saw used in the markets to display food items and other wares--he would carve them or engrave them with Adinkra symbols and other marks using hot rods.[[8]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:4-8) He also began using wood to construct wall panels from strips placed next to each other, the surface decorated with designs imparted on the material through the use of chain saws, gouges, flame, or paint.[[11]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-NMOAA-11) In the late 70s, he began working in clay: pots, in particular, exploring themes of fragility and dilapidation. He was interested in how, even after a pot breaks and ceases being used in the way we commonly think (for food, water), it takes on a new purpose, even acquires more uses, from the mundane to the spiritual. Most intriguing to him is the use of pot shards for presenting offerings. He said, "It's as if the pot, having broken, is transformed into a dimension which makes it ideal for use by ancestors and deities who are themselves in the spirit dimension."[[8]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:4-8)

After his work with the broken pots, Anatsui explored food-adjacent themes in other materials: wood, again, in the form of mortars; equipment used to process [cassava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cassava "Cassava"), and bottle tops.[[8]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:4-8)

Much of Anatsui's work features found materials, or materials that had a life of use prior to being formed into this artworks. His emphasis on the found object, however, is less [Duchampian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marcel_Duchamp "Marcel Duchamp"), and more focused on the history of use and the evidence of the human hand in the material.[[8]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:4-8)

> "When something has been used, there is a certain charge, a certain energy, that has to do with the people who have touched it and used it and sometimes abused it. This helps to direct what one is doing, and also to root what one is doing in the environment and the culture."[[13]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:2-13)

Metal bottle caps are a favorite material of his; like cloth, Anatsui describes, an arrangement of bottle caps is versatile, allowing him to consider his art both sculpturally (through the form of the caps) and in a painterly manner (through the colors of the caps). Further, he appreciates the glimpse that bottle caps give into current and historical political and sociological issues, by virtue of the names and colors of various drink brands that are printed onto the caps.[[13]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:2-13)

> "The most important thing for me is the transformation. The fact that these media, each identifying a brand of drink, are no longer going back to serve the same role but are elements that could generate some reflection, some thinking, or just some wonder. This is possible because they are removed from their accustomed, functional context into a new one, and they bring along their histories and identities."[[8]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:4-8)

A number of themes are present in Anatsui's work: the destruction and subsequent reconstitution of material as a metaphor for life and the changes Africa faced under colonialism and since independence; traditional themes and motifs of West African strip woven cloth and other [African textiles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_textiles "African textiles"); and concern over Western scholarly misinterpretation of African history and the distortions it has caused.[[11]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-NMOAA-11) His work is also thematically connected to the West African cultural landscape and ideas of consumption and labor.[[8]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:4-8)

The idea of [Sankofa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sankofa "Sankofa") [translated as "go back and retrieve"] is also present in Anatsui's work. He views it as a way of drawing on the past, the lessons it offers, to chart a mode of moving forward. For him, Sankofa described a need to draw from what was immediately around him; Ghana became independent when he was in high school, and much of his education had been focused on western art and art history, and so he felt called to 'go back and retrieve' aspects of Ghanaian culture that had been suppressed, something he described as a sort of "quest for self-discovery."[[8]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:4-8)

## Exhibitions

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Exhibitions")]

[![Image 4](http://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/8f/El_Anatsui_-_Man%27s_Cloth.jpg/250px-El_Anatsui_-_Man%27s_Cloth.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:El_Anatsui_-_Man's_Cloth.jpg)

_Man's Cloth_ (1998–2001) at the [British Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Museum "British Museum") in 2009

Anatsui's career grew gradually, starting in his home village of [Nsukka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nsukka "Nsukka") before branching off to places such as [Enugu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enugu_(city) "Enugu (city)") and [Lagos](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lagos "Lagos"), and eventually internationally.[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14) In 1990, Anatsui had his first important group show at the [Studio Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Studio_Museum_in_Harlem "Studio Museum in Harlem") In [Harlem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harlem "Harlem"), [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_(state) "New York (state)"). He also was one of three artists singled out in the 1990 exhibition "Contemporary African Artists: Changing Traditions", which was extended for five years.[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14) Anatsui has since exhibited his work around the world, including at the [Brooklyn Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Museum "Brooklyn Museum") (2013);[[15]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-15) the [Clark Art Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clark_Art_Institute "Clark Art Institute") (2011);[[16]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-16) the Rice University Art Gallery, Houston (2010);[[17]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-17) the [Metropolitan Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metropolitan_Museum_of_Art "Metropolitan Museum of Art"), New York (2008–09);[[18]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-18) the [National Museum of African Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_African_Art "National Museum of African Art"), Smithsonian Institution, Washington, D.C. (2008);[[19]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-19) the [Fowler Museum at UCLA](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fowler_Museum_at_UCLA "Fowler Museum at UCLA") (2007);[[20]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-20) the [Venice Biennale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice_Biennale "Venice Biennale") (1990 and 2007);[[21]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-interview-21) the [Hayward Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hayward_Gallery "Hayward Gallery") (2005);[[22]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-22) the [Liverpool Biennial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Liverpool_Biennial "Liverpool Biennial") (2002);[[21]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-interview-21) the National Museum of African Art (2001);[[21]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-interview-21) the [Centre de Cultura Contemporània de Barcelona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Centre_de_Cultura_Contempor%C3%A0nia_de_Barcelona "Centre de Cultura Contemporània de Barcelona") (2001);[[21]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-interview-21) the 8th Osaka Sculpture Triennale (1995);[[21]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-interview-21) the 5th [Gwangju Biennale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gwangju_Biennale "Gwangju Biennale") (2004); the [Arab Museum of Modern Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_Museum_of_Modern_Art "Arab Museum of Modern Art") in Doha (2019);[[23]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-Lucas_40-23) and the [Kunstmuseum Bern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kunstmuseum_Bern "Kunstmuseum Bern") (2020).[[24]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-24) In 1995, Anatsui held his first solo exhibition outside of Africa in [London](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London "London"). He expressed a variety of themes and demonstrated how African art can be shown in a multitude of ways that are not seen as "typical" African.[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14) His work utilized conceptual modes used by European and American artists but hardly in African countries.[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14) Anatsui showed his work at the de Young Museum in [San Francisco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Francisco "San Francisco") in 2005. This was his first time "appear[ing] as part of the permanent collection in a major art museum".[[25]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:0-25) Also in 2005, his exhibition at New York's [Skoto Gallery](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Skoto_Gallery?action=edit&redlink=1 "Skoto Gallery (page does not exist)"), _Danudo_, was the first display of his metal sheets in an American city.[[25]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:0-25) At this gallery, Skoto Aghahowa presented Anatsui's wood wall panels alongside [Sol LeWitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sol_LeWitt "Sol LeWitt")'s drawings. This exhibition popularized his bottle-cap works as he gained more recognition in the press.[[25]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:0-25)

[![Image 5](http://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/68/Artempo_ElAnatsui.jpg/250px-Artempo_ElAnatsui.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Artempo_ElAnatsui.jpg)

Anatsui's [Palazzo Fortuny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Fortuny "Palazzo Fortuny") Artempo exhibition in 2007

Anatsui was invited to the [Venice Biennale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice_Biennale "Venice Biennale") in 2006 and again in 2007 where he was commissioned to make two hanging metal tapestries. During the 2007 edition, he exhibited his works at the [Palazzo Fortuny](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Palazzo_Fortuny "Palazzo Fortuny") which consisted of newly built walls for him to display three metal hangings entitled _Dusasa_.[[25]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:0-25) Each artwork demonstrated different textures and colors including golds, reds, and blacks. The way the bottle tops draped throughout the hangings created a sense of gentleness that made it stand apart from the other works in the gallery.[[25]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:0-25) The art curator of the Biennale, [Robert Storr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Storr_(art_academic) "Robert Storr (art academic)"), mentions that the artist's series "reaches back into a whole series of things in the postwar period-it has a kind of exaltation I have not seen before".[[25]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:0-25) During this Venetian showing, Anatsui wanted to create a new experience for his viewers conceptually. He believes that "human life is not something which is cut and dried. It is something that is constantly in a state of change."[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14) At this point, he began to refer his metalworks as hangings instead of "cloths".[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14)

[![Image 6](http://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/en/thumb/f/f5/Another_Man%27s_Cloth%2C_2006%2C_El_Anatsui_at_Rubell_DC_2022.jpg/250px-Another_Man%27s_Cloth%2C_2006%2C_El_Anatsui_at_Rubell_DC_2022.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Another_Man's_Cloth,_2006,_El_Anatsui_at_Rubell_DC_2022.jpg)

_Another Man's Cloth_ (2006) at the [Rubell Museum DC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubell_Museum#Rubell_Museum_DC "Rubell Museum") in 2022

A 2010 retrospective of his work, entitled _When I Last Wrote to You About Africa_, was organized by the [Museum for African Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_for_African_Art "Museum for African Art") and opened at the [Royal Ontario Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Royal_Ontario_Museum "Royal Ontario Museum") in [Toronto, Ontario](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toronto "Toronto"), Canada. It subsequently toured venues in the United States for three years, concluding at the [University of Michigan Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Michigan_Museum_of_Art "University of Michigan Museum of Art").

A major exhibition of recent works, entitled _Gravity & Grace: Monumental Works by El Anatsui_, had its [New York](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") premiere at the [Brooklyn Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brooklyn_Museum "Brooklyn Museum") in 2013. Organized by the [Akron Art Museum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akron_Art_Museum "Akron Art Museum") (exhibition: 2012), the exhibition later traveled to the [Des Moines Art Center](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Des_Moines_Art_Center "Des Moines Art Center") (2013–14) and the [Bass Museum of Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bass_Museum "Bass Museum") in Miami (2014).[[26]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-26)

A career-spanning survey of his work, organized by [Okwui Enwezor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Okwui_Enwezor "Okwui Enwezor") and [Chika Okeke-Agulu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chika_Okeke-Agulu "Chika Okeke-Agulu"), entitled _Triumphant Scale_ drew record-breaking crowds when it opened in March 2019, at Munich's [Haus der Kunst](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haus_der_Kunst "Haus der Kunst"). From there, the show travelled to the [Arab Museum of Modern Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_Museum_of_Modern_Art "Arab Museum of Modern Art"), in Doha, and later to the [Kunstmuseum Bern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kunstmuseum_Bern "Kunstmuseum Bern") in 2020.[[23]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-Lucas_40-23)

Anatsui was selected for the 2023 Hyundai Commission at the Turbine Hall at [Tate Modern](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tate_Modern "Tate Modern"); a vast display space for large-scale sculptural and site-specific artworks. His work, _Behind the Red Moon_, is made of thousands of metal bottle tops and fragments, building upon his work with materials linked to the transatlantic slave trade, and was on view through 14 April 2024.[[27]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-27)[[28]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-28)[[29]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-29)

## Other activities

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: Other activities")]

Anatsui was selected to be a member of the International Society for Education through Art (InSEA) world council in 1992 for his work in education.[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14) Anatsui was a founding member and fellow of the [Forum for African Arts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Forum_for_African_Arts?action=edit&redlink=1 "Forum for African Arts (page does not exist)") in 2000. That year he also became a member of the International Selection Committee for the [Dakar Biennale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dakar_Biennale "Dakar Biennale") in Senegal.[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14) In 2001 he was a fellow at the [Civitella Ranieri Foundation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Civitella_Ranieri_Foundation "Civitella Ranieri Foundation") in Italy.[[30]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:1-30)[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14)

## Recognition

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Recognition")]

### Awards

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=El_Anatsui&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Awards")]

Anatsui won an honorable mention at the First [Ghana National Art Competition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghana_National_Art_Competition?action=edit&redlink=1 "Ghana National Art Competition (page does not exist)") as an undergraduate student in 1968. The following year he was awarded the Best Student of the Year at the [College of Art in Kumasi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/College_of_Art_in_Kumasi?action=edit&redlink=1 "College of Art in Kumasi (page does not exist)"), Ghana.[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14) In 1983 he won a commission for two large public sculptures made of terrazzo-surfaced cement on the [Nsukka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nsukka "Nsukka") campus.[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14) He was selected to be one of ten artists invited to the [Zweites Symposium Nordesekkuste](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zweites_Symposium_Nordesekkuste?action=edit&redlink=1 "Zweites Symposium Nordesekkuste (page does not exist)") residency in [Cuxhaven](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cuxhaven "Cuxhaven"), [West Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Germany "West Germany"), in 1984.[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14)

In 1990, Anatsui was invited to the 44th annual [Venice Biennale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice_Biennale "Venice Biennale") show _5 Contemporary African Artists_, where he received an honorable mention.[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14) That year he was included in the American documentary _Nigerian Art-Kindred Spirits_.

In 2015, the Venice Biennale awarded Anatsui the [Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Venice_Biennale#Awards "Venice Biennale").[[31]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-31)[[32]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-32) In 2017, Anatsui was awarded the [Praemium Imperiale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Praemium_Imperiale "Praemium Imperiale"), the first Ghanaian to win this international art prize.[[33]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-33)[[34]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-34)

Other awards include:

*   1990 – Public Prize, 7th Annual Triennale der Kleinplastik[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14)
*   1995 – Kansai Telecasting Prize, 6th Osaka Sculpture Triennial[[30]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:1-30)[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14)
*   1998 – Bronze Prize, 9th Osaka Sculpture Triennial[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14)
*   2008 – Visionaries! Award, [Museum of Arts and Design](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Museum_of_Arts_and_Design "Museum of Arts and Design") (MAD)[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14)
*   2009 – [Prince Claus Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince_Claus_Fund "Prince Claus Fund")
*   2009 – Artist Honoree, 30th Anniversary Celebration, [National Museum of African Art](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Museum_of_African_Art "National Museum of African Art")[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-:03-14)
*   2016 – Honorary doctorate, [Harvard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University")[[35]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-35)[[36]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-36)[[37]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-37)
*   2017 – Honorary doctorate, [Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kwame_Nkrumah_University_of_Science_and_Technology "Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology")[[38]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-38)[[39]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-39)
*   2023 – _[Time 100](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Time\_100 "Time 100")_[[40]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/El_Anatsui#cite_note-40)

**The individual is El Anatsui**  

El Anatsui (born 4 February 1944 in Anyako, Ghana) studied first at the College of Art, Kumasi (KNUST) in Ghana, then continued his artistic development in the United Kingdom and the United States. While teaching in Nigeria he served as Head of Department and later Dean of the Fine Arts Department at the University of Nigeria, Nsukka until 2011. He also founded his own exhibition space that opened in 1995 – a venue that celebrated its 25th anniversary in 2020. The artist was encouraged early in his career to use aluminum bottle‑caps (“bottle‑top” material) as a primary medium, a tool he continued to employ in his work up through 2014.
